units.5: Materials of plant construction, corrosion and material handling

short.q: What is the significance of the Reynolds number?
short.hi: Re se pata chalta hai flow laminar hai ya turbulent

kp.t: Ratio of inertial to viscous forces
Predicts type of flow: laminar / turbulent
Re <2000 laminar, >4000 turbulent

short.a: Reynolds number (Re = Duρ/μ) is the dimensionless ratio of inertial forces to viscous forces. Its significance is that it predicts the type of flow: Re below 2000 = laminar (streamline) flow, 2000-4000 = transition, above 4000 = turbulent flow. It is used in design of pipes, pumps and mixers and to calculate friction losses.

short.q: Define sieve number.
short.hi: Sieve number = 2.54 cm (1 inch) me meshes ki sankhya

kp.t: Number of meshes (openings)
In a length of 2.54 cm / one inch
In each transverse direction parallel to wires

short.a: Sieve number is the number of meshes (openings) present in a length of 2.54 cm (one inch) in each transverse direction parallel to the wires of the sieve. A higher sieve number means smaller openings, i.e. a finer sieve (e.g. sieve no. 120 is finer than sieve no. 10).

short.q: Name the different types of manometers.
short.hi: U-tube, differential, inclined, enlarged leg, inverted

kp.t: Simple U-tube manometer
Differential manometer
Inclined manometer
Enlarged-leg (well type) / inverted / micro manometer

short.a:
A manometer measures pressure difference by balancing it against a column of liquid. Types:
1. Simple U-tube manometer
2. Differential manometer
3. Inclined manometer (for small pressure differences)
4. Enlarged-leg (well type) manometer
5. Inverted U-tube and micro (multiplying) manometer.

short.q: What is a Pitot tube? What does it measure?
short.hi: Pitot tube = kisi point ki local velocity

kp.t: Measures local (point) velocity of fluid
Impact tube facing flow and static tube
u = √(2gh) from manometer reading

short.a: A Pitot tube is a flow-measuring device that measures the local (point) velocity of a fluid in a pipe. It has an impact tube facing the flow and a static tube; the difference between impact (stagnation) pressure and static pressure is read on a manometer, and velocity u = √(2gh).

short.q: Why is a rotameter called a variable area meter?
short.hi: Float upar jaata hai to annular area badhta hai

kp.t: Area of flow (annular space) changes with flow rate
Float rises in tapered tube
Pressure drop remains constant

short.a: In a rotameter the float rises in a vertical tapered tube as the flow rate increases. As it rises, the annular area between the float and the tube wall increases, while the pressure drop across the float stays constant. Since the flow area varies with flow rate, it is called a variable area meter.

short.q: Define size reduction. Give any two objectives.
short.hi: Comminution: surface area badhana, mixing aasan

kp.t: Breaking solids into smaller particles (comminution)
Increases surface area / dissolution
Uniform mixing / extraction / drying

short.a:
Size reduction (comminution) is the process of reducing large solid particles into smaller particles by mechanical means (cutting, crushing, impact, grinding).
Objectives: (1) increases surface area, so dissolution and absorption improve; (2) helps uniform mixing and content uniformity; also aids extraction of crude drugs and drying.

short.q: State Rittinger's law and Kick's law of size reduction.
short.hi: Rittinger: new surface; Kick: reduction ratio

kp.t: Rittinger: energy ∝ new surface area created
Kick: energy ∝ size reduction ratio
Rittinger for fine, Kick for coarse grinding

short.a:
Rittinger's law: the work required for size reduction is proportional to the new surface area created, E = KR(1/D2 - 1/D1); applies to fine grinding.
Kick's law: the energy required is proportional to the size reduction ratio, E = KK ln(D1/D2); applies to coarse crushing.

short.q: Name the mechanisms of size reduction with one example of mill for each.
short.hi: Cutting, compression, impact, attrition

kp.t: Cutting - cutter mill
Compression - roller / end runner mill
Impact - hammer mill
Attrition - fluid energy / edge runner mill

short.a:
1. Cutting - cutter (knife) mill
2. Compression (crushing) - roller mill, end runner mill
3. Impact - hammer mill
4. Attrition (rubbing/shear) - fluid energy mill, edge runner mill
Ball mill works by both impact and attrition.

short.q: What is the critical speed of a ball mill?
short.hi: Critical speed par balls wall se chipak jaati hain

kp.t: Speed at which balls just start centrifuging
Balls move with wall, no grinding
Optimum speed is 1/2 to 3/4 of critical speed

short.a: Critical speed of a ball mill is the speed of rotation at which the balls just begin to centrifuge, i.e. they are carried around with the wall of the cylinder and no grinding occurs. Nc = 0.5/√(R - r) rps (R = mill radius, r = ball radius, in metres). Ball mills are operated at about one-half to three-fourth of the critical speed for effective grinding.

short.q: Give two uses of fluid energy mill.
short.hi: Micronization: ultra-fine, heat-sensitive powders

kp.t: Ultra-fine grinding / micronization
Heat-sensitive (thermolabile) drugs
Example: antibiotics, vitamins, steroids

short.a:
Fluid energy mill (jet mill / micronizer) is used:
1. To reduce particles to a very fine size (micronization, about 1-30 micron), e.g. for aerosols and injections.
2. To grind heat-sensitive (thermolabile) drugs such as antibiotics and vitamins, because the expanding air cools the material.
It also gives a contamination-free product.

short.q: Define elutriation.
short.hi: Upward fluid stream se particles ko size ke hisaab se alag karna

kp.t: Size separation in an upward moving fluid
Particles settle by settling velocity / Stokes law
Fine particles carried over, coarse settle

short.a: Elutriation is a method of size separation in which particles are separated by an upward moving stream of fluid (water or air). Particles whose settling velocity (by Stokes' law) is less than the fluid velocity are carried upward and overflow, while larger, heavier particles settle down. It is done in an elutriation tank.

short.q: Explain Bernoulli's theorem and its pharmaceutical applications.
short.hi: Total energy (pressure + kinetic + potential) constant रहती है

kp.t: Total energy of flowing fluid remains constant
Pressure head + velocity head + potential head
Steady, incompressible, non-viscous fluid assumption
Applications: venturimeter, orifice meter, Pitot tube

short.a:
Bernoulli's theorem: in steady flow of an ideal (incompressible, non-viscous) fluid, the total energy at any point is constant. Total energy = pressure energy + kinetic energy + potential energy.
P/ρg + u²/2g + Z = constant (pressure head + velocity head + potential head).
Applications:
1. Basis of flow meters: venturimeter, orifice meter, Pitot tube
2. Calculation of energy losses and pump work in pipelines
3. Working of atomisers, sprayers and aspirators (filter pumps), and design of pipelines that carry liquids in pharmaceutical plants.

short.q: Differentiate between orifice meter and venturimeter.
short.hi: Venturi me pressure loss kam, orifice sasta aur chhota

kp.t: Orifice: thin plate with hole; venturi: converging-throat-diverging tube
Venturi has low permanent pressure loss; orifice high
Orifice cheap and small; venturi costly and long
Coefficient of discharge: orifice ~0.61, venturi ~0.98

short.a:
Both work on Bernoulli's theorem (velocity increases, pressure falls at a constriction).
1. Orifice meter: a thin plate with a sharp-edged hole fixed in the pipe. Venturimeter: a tube with converging cone, throat and gradually diverging cone.
2. Orifice has large permanent pressure (energy) loss; venturi has very small loss because pressure is recovered in the diverging part.
3. Coefficient of discharge: orifice about 0.61; venturi about 0.98.
4. Orifice is cheap, easy to install and change, needs little space; venturi is costly, long and difficult to change.

short.q: Write a note on edge runner mill and end runner mill.
short.hi: Edge runner = crushing + shear; End runner = mortar-pestle jaisa

kp.t: Edge runner: heavy stone/steel rollers on stone bed
Edge runner works by crushing (compression) and shearing
End runner: rotating mortar with weighted pestle
End runner works by crushing (compression) and shear
Slow mills for fine grinding of drugs

short.a:
Edge runner mill: one or two heavy rollers (stone or granite) move on a stationary stone bed (or the bed rotates). Material is fed on the bed and is size-reduced by crushing (compression due to heavy weight of rollers) and shearing. A scraper keeps material in the path of the rollers. Uses: fine grinding of crude drugs.
End runner mill: works like a mechanical mortar and pestle. A steel mortar (bowl) rotates and a heavy weighted pestle, placed off-centre, rotates by friction. Size reduction is by crushing and shear.
Demerits of both: slow, noisy, occupy large space, high power, not for sticky materials.

short.q: Explain the principle, construction and working of a cyclone separator. Give its merits and demerits.
short.hi: Cyclone = centrifugal force se solid particles gas se alag

kp.t: Principle: centrifugal force separates particles
Tangential inlet into cylinder with conical base
Heavy particles hit wall and fall to bottom
Clean air leaves through central top outlet

short.a:
Principle: the cyclone separator uses centrifugal force (and gravity) to separate solid particles from a gas (or liquid).
Construction: a short vertical cylinder with a conical lower part, a tangential inlet near the top, a central outlet pipe at the top for air and an outlet at the bottom of the cone for solids.
Working: air with suspended particles enters tangentially and moves in a spiral (vortex). Heavier, larger particles are thrown to the wall by centrifugal force, lose speed and fall into the cone. Clean air forms an inner vortex and leaves through the top.
Uses: separating dust, collecting spray-dried product. Merit: no moving parts, cheap. Demerit: poor for very fine particles.

short.q: Explain the factors affecting size reduction.
short.hi: Hardness, toughness, moisture, stickiness, temperature असर करते हैं

kp.t: Hardness of material
Toughness / elasticity
Moisture content
Stickiness
Heat sensitivity / softening temperature
Abrasiveness and purity required

short.a:
1. Hardness: harder materials (high Mohs number) need more energy.
2. Toughness: tough, fibrous or elastic materials (e.g. barks, roots, rubber) are difficult to grind; cooling or wetting may help.
3. Moisture content: wet material sticks and clogs the mill; generally less than about 5% moisture is preferred for dry milling.
4. Stickiness: sticky materials (gums, resins) adhere to mill surfaces.
5. Softening temperature: waxy and heat-sensitive drugs soften or decompose due to heat produced; cold milling is used.
6. Abrasiveness, physiological effect of dust and purity required also decide the choice of mill.

short.q: Explain the principle, construction and working of a rotameter.
short.hi: Rotameter = variable area meter, tapered tube me float upar uthta hai

kp.t: Variable area meter (constant pressure drop)
Vertical tapered glass tube
Float rises with flow rate
Float position read on scale = flow rate

short.a:
Principle: rotameter is a variable area flow meter. The pressure drop across the float stays constant while the area of flow (annular space) changes with flow rate.
Construction: a vertical, tapered (wider at top) transparent glass tube with a float inside; the tube carries a graduated scale.
Working: fluid enters from the bottom and lifts the float. The float rises until the upward drag force balances its weight; the annular area increases as it rises. The height of the float on the scale gives flow rate directly.
Merits: direct reading, simple, cheap. Demerits: must be vertical, glass is fragile, not for opaque fluids.

short.q: List any two factors that influence evaporation.
short.hi: Temperature, pressure, surface area, viscosity, foaming

kp.t: Temperature / thermolability of product
Pressure (vacuum lowers boiling point)
Surface area, agitation, viscosity, foaming, scale

short.a:
Factors influencing evaporation:
1. Temperature and heat sensitivity of the product (thermolabile drugs need low temperature).
2. Pressure: reduced pressure (vacuum) lowers the boiling point and allows evaporation at low temperature.
Others: surface area of liquid, agitation, viscosity/concentration, foaming, scale (deposit) formation and time of heating.

short.q: State the basic principle of distillation.
short.hi: Boiling point/volatility ke difference se separation

kp.t: Separation based on difference in volatility / boiling point
Liquid converted to vapour by heating
Vapour condensed back to liquid (distillate)

short.a: Distillation is the separation of components of a liquid mixture by converting the liquid into vapour by heating and then condensing the vapour back into liquid (distillate). It is based on the difference in volatility (vapour pressure / boiling point) of the components; the more volatile component is richer in the vapour (Raoult's law).

short.q: Write two differences between simple and fractional distillation.
short.hi: Fractional me fractionating column, close boiling points

kp.t: Simple: no fractionating column; fractional uses column
Simple: boiling points differ widely; fractional: close boiling points
Fractional: repeated vaporisation-condensation / reflux, better separation

short.a:
1. Simple distillation is done without a fractionating column; fractional distillation uses a fractionating column between flask and condenser.
2. Simple distillation separates liquids whose boiling points differ widely (or a volatile liquid from non-volatile solids); fractional distillation separates miscible liquids with close boiling points.
3. In fractional distillation repeated vaporisation-condensation (reflux) occurs in the column, so separation is much better.

short.q: What is flash distillation?
short.hi: Achanak pressure kam karke liquid ka ek hissa vapour

kp.t: Liquid heated under pressure
Sudden pressure reduction - part vaporises (flashes)
Vapour and liquid in equilibrium separated (equilibrium distillation)

short.a: Flash distillation (equilibrium distillation) is a process in which a liquid mixture is heated under pressure and then its pressure is suddenly reduced through a valve into a separator. A part of the liquid suddenly vaporises (flashes); the vapour and remaining liquid, which are in equilibrium, are separated. Used for multicomponent mixtures such as petroleum crude and for liquids with widely different boiling points.

short.q: State Fourier's law of heat conduction.
short.hi: Heat flow ∝ area × temperature gradient

kp.t: Rate of heat flow ∝ area
∝ temperature gradient (dt/dx)
dQ/dθ = -kA dt/dx, k thermal conductivity

short.a:
Fourier's law states that the rate of heat flow by conduction through a uniform material is directly proportional to the area normal to heat flow and to the temperature gradient in the direction of heat flow.
dQ/dθ = -k A dt/dx, where k = thermal conductivity, A = area, dt/dx = temperature gradient. The negative sign shows heat flows from higher to lower temperature.

short.q: State Stefan-Boltzmann law of radiation.
short.hi: Black body radiation ∝ T⁴

kp.t: Energy emitted by black body
Proportional to fourth power of absolute temperature
E = σT⁴, Stefan constant

short.a:
Stefan-Boltzmann law states that the total energy radiated per unit area per unit time by a black body is directly proportional to the fourth power of its absolute temperature.
E = σ T⁴, where σ = Stefan-Boltzmann constant (5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W/m²K⁴). For real (grey) bodies E = ε σ T⁴ (ε = emissivity).

short.q: Differentiate between heat exchangers and heat interchangers.
short.hi: Exchanger: steam/gas → liquid; Interchanger: liquid → liquid

kp.t: Heat exchanger: heat from hot gas or steam to a liquid
Heat interchanger: liquid to liquid or gas to gas
Both through a metal wall (no mixing)

short.a:
Heat exchangers are devices used for transferring heat from one fluid (hot gas or steam) to another fluid (liquid) through a metal wall, e.g. steam heated shell and tube exchanger.
Heat interchangers are devices used for transferring heat from one liquid to another liquid or from one gas to another gas through a metal wall, e.g. hot product cooling incoming feed (heat recovery). In both the fluids do not mix.

short.q: Define economy of a multiple effect evaporator.
short.hi: Economy = kg vapour / kg steam

kp.t: Kg of water vaporised per kg of steam used
Increases with number of effects
Capacity not increased by adding effects

short.a: Economy of an evaporator is the kilograms of water (vapour) evaporated per kilogram of steam supplied. In a single effect it is less than 1. In a multiple effect evaporator the vapour of one effect heats the next, so economy increases roughly in proportion to the number of effects, while the total capacity (evaporation per unit time) is not increased.

short.q: What is the principle of molecular distillation?
short.hi: Very high vacuum, gap < mean free path

kp.t: Very high vacuum
Condenser distance less than mean free path
Molecules reach condenser without collision; for heat-sensitive, high mol wt substances

short.a: In molecular (short path) distillation, a very high vacuum is applied and the distance between the evaporating surface and the condensing surface is kept less than the mean free path of the vapour molecules. Molecules escaping from the liquid reach the condenser without colliding with other molecules and condense. It is used for heat-sensitive, high molecular weight substances, e.g. vitamin A from fish liver oil.

short.q: Explain the principle and working of a climbing film evaporator.
short.hi: Steam se boiling, vapour liquid ko thin film me upar le jaata hai

kp.t: Principle: liquid rises as thin film carried by vapour
Long vertical tubes in steam jacket (calandria)
Feed enters at bottom, boils, vapour drags liquid up
Separator (cyclone/vapour head) at top
Short contact time - thermolabile; good for foaming
Demerits: not for viscous liquids, costly, hard to clean

short.a:
Principle: the liquid is heated in long vertical tubes by steam. Boiling starts at the bottom; the vapour formed moves up rapidly and drags the liquid as a thin film along the tube walls. The thin film and high velocity give rapid heat transfer and short contact time.
Construction: a steam-jacketed bundle of long vertical tubes (calandria), feed inlet at the bottom, and a vapour head with separator (cyclone/deflector) at the top; concentrated liquor outlet and vapour line to condenser.
Working: preheated feed enters at the bottom, boils, and climbs as a film; at the top the concentrate is separated from vapour; it may be recycled.
Uses: concentration of thermolabile products (insulin, liver extract, vitamins) and foaming liquids.
Demerits: not suitable for viscous liquids, costly, difficult to clean, needs careful feed control.

short.q: Discuss the principle and working of fractional distillation.
short.hi: Fractionating column me baar baar vaporisation-condensation

kp.t: Used for miscible liquids with close boiling points
Raoult's law: vapour richer in more volatile component
Fractionating column between flask and condenser
Repeated vaporisation-condensation, reflux, theoretical plates
Applications: alcohol, petroleum, solvent purification

a.intro: Fractional distillation is the separation of a mixture of miscible liquids whose boiling points are close to each other, using a fractionating column.
points: Principle: according to Raoult's law, the vapour above a liquid mixture is richer in the more volatile component. When this vapour is condensed and re-vaporised again and again, it becomes progressively richer in the more volatile component.

Construction: a distillation flask (still) heated from below, a fractionating column (packed with glass beads/rings, or with bubble-cap or sieve plates) fitted above it, a thermometer at the top, a condenser and receivers.

Working: vapour rising through the column meets the descending liquid (reflux). At each stage (plate) heat exchange causes partial condensation of the less volatile component and vaporisation of the more volatile one.
The more volatile component collects at the top and is condensed; the less volatile component returns to the still. Fractions are collected at different temperature ranges.
Reflux ratio and number of theoretical plates decide the efficiency of separation.
Applications: separation of acetone-methanol, purification of alcohol, petroleum refining, recovery and purification of solvents.
a.diagram: Round bottom flask on heater, vertical fractionating column with packing above it, thermometer at the top, side arm to a water condenser and receiver.
a.conclusion: Fractional distillation gives sharp separation of liquids with close boiling points because of repeated vaporisation-condensation in the column.

short.q: Explain the principle, construction and working of a steam jacketed kettle. Give its merits and demerits.
short.hi: Hemispherical pan + steam jacket; open evaporation

kp.t: Hemispherical pan surrounded by steam jacket
Steam inlet, condensate outlet, vent for air
Made of copper or stainless steel
Uses: concentration of aqueous extracts / liquids
Merits: simple, cheap, easy to clean
Demerits: small heating area, open (vapour in room), not for solvents/thermolabile

short.a:
Principle: heat is transferred from steam in the jacket through the metal wall to the liquid in the pan, which boils and evaporates at atmospheric pressure.
Construction: a hemispherical (or deep) pan of copper, stainless steel or enamelled iron surrounded by an outer jacket. The jacket has a steam inlet at the top, a condensate outlet at the bottom and a vent for non-condensable gases. A product outlet is at the bottom of the pan; small kettles may be tilting.
Working: steam enters the jacket and condenses on the wall, giving its latent heat; the liquid boils and vapour escapes into the room; contents may be stirred.
Uses: concentration of aqueous liquids and extracts (e.g. liquorice).
Merits: simple, cheap, easy to clean and operate.
Demerits: small heating area compared to volume, open vessel (vapour enters room), not suitable for organic solvents or thermolabile products, heating area falls as liquid concentrates.

short.q: Explain the principle and methodology of steam distillation. Give its applications.
short.hi: Immiscible liquids: total vapour pressure = sum; 100°C se kam par boil

kp.t: For immiscible liquids (with water)
Total vapour pressure = sum of individual vapour pressures
Mixture boils below 100 °C / below boiling point of either
Steam passed through material, distillate separates into layers
Applications: volatile oils, e.g. clove, eucalyptus

short.a:
Principle: when two immiscible liquids are heated together, each exerts its own vapour pressure independently, and the total vapour pressure is the sum of the two (P = PA + PB). The mixture boils when this total equals atmospheric pressure, i.e. at a temperature below the boiling point of either liquid (below 100 °C with water).
Methodology: steam from a steam generator is passed into a flask containing the material (e.g. crushed plant drug with water). The volatile substance distils with steam at below 100 °C, is condensed, and the distillate separates into oil and water layers, which are separated (Florentine receiver/separating funnel).
Applications: extraction of volatile (essential) oils such as clove, eucalyptus and peppermint oil; purification of high boiling heat-sensitive substances immiscible with water (e.g. camphor).

short.q: Differentiate evaporation from other heat processes such as drying, distillation and crystallization.
short.hi: Evaporation me product concentrated liquid hota hai

kp.t: Evaporation: removes solvent to give concentrated liquid
Drying: final product is solid with low moisture
Distillation: vapour is condensed and collected (product)
Crystallization: aim is crystals from solution
Evaporation done at boiling point; drying below boiling

short.a:
1. Evaporation vs drying: evaporation removes a volatile solvent (usually water) from a solution to give a concentrated liquid (thick extract); drying removes moisture to give a solid product with low residual moisture. Evaporation occurs at the boiling point of the liquid, while drying usually occurs below it, at the surface.
2. Evaporation vs distillation: in evaporation the vapour is discarded and the concentrate is the product; in distillation the vapour is condensed and collected as the product (distillate), or components are separated.
3. Evaporation vs crystallization: evaporation stops before crystals form (concentrate is the product); in crystallization the aim is to form pure crystals from a supersaturated solution.

short.q: Give two applications of a ribbon blender.
short.hi: Ribbon blender: powders aur wet masses mixing

kp.t: Mixing / blending of dry powders
Mixing of wet masses in granulation / pastes
Horizontal trough with helical ribbons

short.a:
A ribbon blender is a horizontal trough with helical ribbon agitators rotating inside.
Applications:
1. Mixing (blending) of finely divided dry powders, e.g. tablet and capsule powder blends.
2. Mixing of wet solid masses for wet granulation and of pasty materials.
It is also used for solid-liquid mixing (spraying a liquid onto powders).

short.q: Write one application of freeze drying.
short.hi: Freeze drying: antibiotics, vaccines, plasma

kp.t: Drying of thermolabile products
Antibiotics, vaccines, sera, plasma, proteins, enzymes
Dry powder for reconstitution / injections

short.a: Freeze drying (lyophilisation) is used to dry thermolabile products such as antibiotics (e.g. dry powder injections for reconstitution), vaccines, sera, blood plasma, proteins, enzymes and hormones. The porous dry product dissolves quickly when water is added.

short.q: Define equilibrium moisture content.
short.hi: EMC: na moisture le, na de — hawa ke saath equilibrium

kp.t: Moisture content in equilibrium with surrounding air
At given temperature and relative humidity
Material neither gains nor loses moisture / limit of drying

short.a: Equilibrium moisture content (EMC) is the moisture content of a material when it is in equilibrium with the surrounding air of a given temperature and relative humidity, i.e. the material neither gains nor loses moisture. It is the lowest moisture content to which a material can be dried under those air conditions.

short.q: Define critical moisture content and free moisture content.
short.hi: CMC par constant rate khatam, falling rate shuru

kp.t: CMC: moisture at end of constant rate period
Falling rate period begins at CMC
Free moisture = total moisture - EMC

short.a:
Critical moisture content (CMC) is the moisture content at which the constant rate period of drying ends and the falling rate period begins.
Free moisture content is the moisture that can be removed by drying under given conditions; it equals the total moisture content minus the equilibrium moisture content.

short.q: Name two tumbling blenders and give their principle.
short.hi: Double cone aur V (twin shell) blender — tumbling

kp.t: Double cone blender
Twin shell (V-) blender
Principle: tumbling, mainly diffusive mixing

short.a:
1. Double cone blender: two cones joined at their bases, rotated about a horizontal axis.
2. Twin shell (V-) blender: two cylinders joined to form a V, rotated about a horizontal axis.
Principle: tumbling motion; as the vessel rotates, powder is repeatedly split, cascades and recombines, giving mainly diffusive (and some convective) mixing of free-flowing powders.

short.q: Write the principle and uses of a sigma blade mixer.
short.hi: Do sigma blades kneading/shear se mix karte hain

kp.t: Two sigma-shaped blades in a double trough
Rotate towards each other at different speeds - shearing and kneading
Uses: wet granulation masses, ointments, pastes

short.a:
Principle: shearing and kneading. Two heavy sigma (S)-shaped blades rotate towards each other at different speeds in a double (W-shaped) trough, so the mass is sheared and kneaded.
Uses: mixing of wet masses for granulation, ointments, pastes and other plastic or sticky semisolid materials. The trough is tilted for unloading.

short.q: Give the principle of the Silverson emulsifier.
short.hi: Rotor-stator: high speed, high shear

kp.t: High speed rotor inside a stator (mixing head)
Liquid drawn in by suction, forced through stator holes
Intense shear breaks droplets - fine emulsion

short.a: The Silverson emulsifier (mixer-homogeniser) works on a rotor-stator principle. A high speed rotor turns inside a fixed stator having fine holes or slots. The rotor draws liquids into the head by suction and throws them out through the stator openings at high velocity, producing intense hydraulic and mechanical shear that breaks droplets into very fine size, giving a stable emulsion.

short.q: Explain the principle, construction, working, uses, merits and demerits of spray dryer.
short.hi: Atomizer se fine droplets, hot air me seconds me dry

kp.t: Principle: atomisation into fine droplets in hot air
Huge surface area - drying in few seconds
Construction: drying chamber, atomiser (disc/nozzle), heater, cyclone
Product: spherical, hollow, free-flowing particles
Uses: acacia, gelatin, lactose, extracts, milk, antibiotics
Demerits: bulky, costly, low thermal efficiency

a.intro: Spray drying converts a liquid feed (solution, suspension or emulsion) directly into a dry powder in a single step.
points: Principle: the fluid is atomised into fine droplets in a hot gas stream. The very large surface area gives rapid evaporation; drying is complete within a few seconds, and the droplet temperature stays near the wet-bulb temperature, so heat-sensitive drugs are protected.

Construction: a large stainless steel drying chamber with conical bottom; an atomiser at the top (rotating disc or pressure/two-fluid nozzle); an air heater and fan for hot air inlet; a cyclone separator (and bag filter) to collect the product.

Working: feed is pumped to the atomiser and sprayed as fine droplets; hot air enters the chamber and dries the droplets as they fall; dry particles separate from air in the chamber bottom and cyclone.
Uses: drying of acacia, gelatin, lactose, milk products, plant extracts, antibiotics, enzymes and vitamins; microencapsulation; preparing directly compressible excipients.
Merits: continuous, very rapid drying suitable for thermolabile materials, product is spherical, hollow, uniform and free flowing with good solubility, direct powder from liquid (no milling).
Demerits: bulky and expensive equipment, low thermal efficiency, product has low bulk density, not suitable for small batches.
a.diagram: Tall cylindrical chamber with conical base; atomiser at top; hot air inlet with heater and fan; outlet duct from base to a cyclone separator with product collector.
a.conclusion: Spray drying is preferred for converting heat-sensitive liquids directly to free flowing powders.

short.q: Explain the principle, construction and working of a planetary mixer with its merits and demerits.
short.hi: Blade apni axis + bowl ke around ghoomta hai (planetary)

kp.t: Planetary motion: blade rotates on own axis and revolves round bowl
Shear / kneading action, covers whole bowl
Bowl and beater/whisk/hook blades; speed variable
Uses: wet granulation, creams, pastes, semisolids
Demerits: limited capacity, heat, high power

short.a:
Principle: the mixing blade rotates about its own axis and at the same time revolves around the central axis of the bowl (planetary motion). This gives shear and kneading action and the blade reaches every part of the bowl.
Construction: a stationary removable stainless steel bowl and a vertical shaft carrying a blade (flat beater, whisk or dough hook), driven by gears; speed can be changed; bowl can be raised or lowered.
Working: material is loaded in the bowl, the blade moves in a planetary path, mixing by shearing and kneading; the bowl is lowered to discharge.
Uses: wet granulation masses, creams, ointments, pastes and other semisolids.
Merits: variable speed, efficient mixing of viscous materials, easy cleaning.
Demerits: limited batch capacity, mechanical heat produced, high power for stiff masses, a dead zone may remain near the bowl bottom.

short.q: Explain the principle, construction and working of a tray dryer. Give its uses, merits and demerits.
short.hi: Tray dryer: hot air trays ke upar circulate

kp.t: Principle: hot air circulated over wet material on trays (convection)
Cabinet with trays on shelves, heaters and fan
Air partly recirculated; baffles for uniform flow
Uses: granules, crude drugs, chemicals, small batches
Demerits: long drying time, labour, uneven drying

short.a:
Principle: hot air is circulated across the wet material spread on trays; heat transfer is by convection and moisture is carried away by the air.
Construction: an insulated rectangular cabinet with shelves holding shallow trays, electric or steam heaters, a fan to circulate air, and adjustable air inlet and outlet with baffles for uniform air flow.
Working: wet material is spread in thin layers on trays loaded on the shelves; fresh air is heated and blown over the trays; part of the moist air is exhausted and the rest recirculated with fresh air until drying is complete.
Uses: drying of granules, crude drugs, chemicals, sticky and small batch materials.
Merits: simple, each batch handled separately (easy to avoid cross-contamination), versatile.
Demerits: long drying time, labour intensive loading/unloading, uneven drying, high heat loss.

short.q: Explain the principle, construction and working of a drum dryer with its uses, merits and demerits.
short.hi: Garam rotating drum par thin film, doctor knife se kharoch

kp.t: Heated rotating drum, steam inside
Thin film of liquid on drum surface dries in one revolution
Doctor knife scrapes dried product
Uses: milk products, starch, extracts, slurries
Merits: rapid, short heat exposure; demerits: not for salts forming scale, skilled operation

short.a:
Principle: a thin film of liquid feed is spread on the outer surface of a heated rotating drum; heat is conducted through the drum wall and the film dries during less than one revolution.
Construction: a horizontal hollow metal drum (single or double), heated internally by steam, rotating slowly; a feed pan or spreader below/above the drum; a doctor knife pressed against the drum to scrape the dry product into a conveyor or bin.
Working: the drum dips into the feed pan and picks up a thin film; the film dries as the drum rotates; the doctor knife removes the dried film as flakes.
Uses: drying of solutions and slurries, e.g. milk products, starch products, malt extract.
Merits: rapid drying, short heat exposure, compact, continuous.
Demerits: not suitable for materials that are very heat-sensitive or that form sticky films, operating conditions need skill, product is in flake form and may need milling.

short.q: Explain the principle, construction and working of a vacuum dryer. Give its uses, merits and demerits.
short.hi: Vacuum me low temperature par drying

kp.t: Drying under reduced pressure at low temperature
Jacketed chamber with hollow heated shelves
Condenser and vacuum pump
Uses: thermolabile, hygroscopic, easily oxidised drugs, solvent recovery
Demerits: batch, costly, slow heat transfer

short.a:
Principle: under reduced pressure water (or solvent) evaporates at a lower temperature; heat is supplied by conduction from heated shelves.
Construction: a heavy cast iron or steel chamber (vacuum oven) with a tightly closing door, containing hollow shelves through which steam or hot water flows; trays rest on the shelves; the chamber is connected to a condenser and a vacuum pump.
Working: trays with wet material are placed on shelves, the door is closed, vacuum is applied and the shelves heated; vapour is condensed in the condenser.
Uses: thermolabile, hygroscopic and easily oxidised materials; drying with solvent recovery; drying of extracts.
Merits: low temperature drying, no oxidation (no air), solvent can be recovered, no dust.
Demerits: batch process, costly, low capacity, slow heat transfer (only conduction), labour intensive.

short.q: What are filter aids? Give two examples.
short.hi: Filter aid = porous cake banata hai, e.g. kieselguhr

kp.t: Inert substances forming porous, permeable cake
Prevent clogging by fine/slimy solids, increase rate
Examples: diatomite (kieselguhr), perlite, cellulose, asbestos, charcoal

short.a:
Filter aids are inert, insoluble, porous substances that form a highly permeable cake and prevent fine or slimy (gelatinous) solids from blocking the filter medium, so the filtration rate increases. They are used as a precoat on the medium or added to the slurry (body feed).
Examples: diatomaceous earth (kieselguhr), perlite, cellulose fibres, asbestos, activated charcoal, talc.

short.q: Name the different types of filter media with examples.
short.hi: Woven cloth, metal mesh, sintered, membrane, paper

kp.t: Woven fabrics: cotton, nylon, silk
Metal screens / wire mesh, perforated sheets
Non-woven: paper, felt, asbestos pads
Sintered glass/metal, porcelain; membranes

short.a:
Filter medium is the porous material that retains solids and allows liquid to pass.
1. Woven fabrics: cotton, wool, silk, nylon, terylene cloth.
2. Metal: stainless steel wire mesh, perforated metal sheets, metafilter rings.
3. Non-woven: filter paper, felt, asbestos and cellulose pads.
4. Rigid porous media: sintered glass, sintered metal, porcelain, ceramics.
5. Membrane filters: cellulose esters, nylon, PTFE.

short.q: State Darcy's law of filtration.
short.hi: Rate ∝ area × pressure difference / (viscosity × cake thickness)

kp.t: Rate of filtration ∝ area and pressure drop
Inversely ∝ viscosity and thickness of cake
V/t = K A ΔP / (μ L), K = permeability

short.a:
Darcy's law states that the rate of flow of liquid through a porous bed (filter cake and medium) is directly proportional to the area and the pressure difference across the bed, and inversely proportional to the viscosity of the liquid and the thickness of the bed.
V/t = K A ΔP / (μ L), where K = permeability coefficient of the bed.

short.q: Write the principle of a metafilter.
short.hi: Metal rings ke beech ke chhote gaps se filtration

kp.t: Stack of metal rings on grooved rod
Narrow gaps between rings act as filter medium (surface filtration)
Filter aid bed (kieselguhr) deposited for fine filtration
Uses: clarification of syrups, elixirs, injections

short.a: A metafilter consists of a series of thin stainless steel rings with small projections on one face, stacked on a grooved rod. The narrow gaps between the rings act as the filtering surface; the filtrate passes between rings, travels along the grooves of the rod and leaves. A bed of filter aid (e.g. kieselguhr) is usually deposited on the rings for very fine filtration. Used for clarification of syrups, elixirs and injection solutions; it is strong, can be sterilised and cleaned by back-flushing.

short.q: What is a cartridge filter? Give its uses.
short.hi: Housing me replaceable cylindrical filter cartridge

kp.t: Cylindrical cartridge in a housing
Pleated membrane / wound fibre / depth media
Uses: sterile filtration, clarification of liquids, air/gas
Disposable, easy to change, large area

short.a:
A cartridge filter is a cylindrical filter element (cartridge) placed inside a closed housing. The cartridge may be a pleated membrane, wound fibre or depth medium of polypropylene, cellulose, PTFE etc. Liquid enters the housing, passes through the cartridge from outside to inside and leaves through the central core.
Uses: sterile filtration of parenterals and ophthalmic solutions (0.22 µm), clarification of liquids, filtration of air and gases.
Merits: large area in small space, disposable, quick to change, no leakage.

short.q: What is a filter leaf? Give its principle.
short.hi: Wire frame + cloth, slurry me dubo kar vacuum

kp.t: Frame of grooved plate or wire mesh covered with filter cloth
Immersed in slurry; vacuum or pressure applied
Cake forms on outer surface; filtrate through drain pipe
Simple, for small batches / dilute slurries

short.a: A filter leaf is the simplest filter: a frame (grooved plate or wire mesh) covered with filter cloth, with a drain pipe. It is immersed in the slurry and vacuum (or pressure) is applied; filtrate passes through the cloth and out of the pipe, while solids form a cake on the outer surface. Simple and cheap; used for small batches and dilute slurries.

short.q: Define relative centrifugal force (RCF).
short.hi: RCF = centrifugal force / gravity = ω²r/g

kp.t: Ratio of centrifugal force to gravity
RCF = ω²r/g
RCF = 1.118 × 10⁻⁵ r N² (r in cm, N in rpm)

short.a:
Relative centrifugal force (RCF) is the ratio of the centrifugal force acting on a particle in a centrifuge to the force of gravity, i.e. how many times g the particle experiences.
RCF = ω²r / g = 1.118 × 10⁻⁵ × r × N², where r = radius in cm and N = speed in rpm. It increases with the square of speed.

short.q: Differentiate between perforated and non-perforated basket centrifuge.
short.hi: Perforated: filtration; non-perforated: sedimentation

kp.t: Perforated: basket wall has holes lined with filter cloth
Perforated works by centrifugal filtration
Non-perforated: solid wall, works by sedimentation
Non-perforated: liquid removed by skimming tube
Uses: perforated for crystals; non-perforated for fine/soft solids that clog cloth

short.a:
1. Construction: perforated basket centrifuge has a vertical basket with a perforated wall lined with filter cloth or screen; non-perforated basket centrifuge has a solid (imperforate) wall.
2. Principle: perforated works by centrifugal filtration - liquid passes through the cake and holes, solids are retained as cake; non-perforated works by centrifugal sedimentation - solids settle on the wall and clear liquid forms an inner layer.
3. Removal of liquid: in perforated, filtrate leaves through the holes into the outer casing; in non-perforated, clear liquid is removed by a skimming tube or overflow.
4. Uses: perforated for separating crystals from mother liquor and drying granules/crystals (cake can be washed); non-perforated for fine, soft or deformable solids that would clog a cloth, and for clarification of liquids.
5. Cake: perforated gives a drier, washed cake; non-perforated gives a wetter sludge.

short.q: Explain the principle, construction and working of a rotary drum filter. Give its uses, merits and demerits.
short.hi: Vacuum drum continuous: filtration, washing, drying, scraping

kp.t: Continuous vacuum filtration
Horizontal drum covered with cloth, partly submerged in slurry trough
Sectors connected to rotary valve
Zones: pick-up, washing, drying, cake removal
Cake removed by doctor knife / strings
Uses: slurries with high solids, antibiotic broths; demerit: costly, limited pressure

a.intro: A rotary drum filter is a continuous vacuum filter used for slurries with a high proportion of solids.
points: Principle: a slowly rotating drum covered with filter cloth dips into the slurry; vacuum inside draws liquid through the cloth and solids form a cake that is washed, dried and removed in one revolution.

Construction: a horizontal metal drum with a perforated surface covered by filter cloth; its inside is divided into sectors, each connected by pipes to a rotary valve that applies vacuum or air at the correct time; the lower part of the drum dips in a slurry trough with agitator; wash sprays and a doctor knife (or string discharge) are fitted.

Working: (1) pick-up/filtration zone - the submerged part sucks filtrate and forms cake; (2) washing zone - water sprays wash the cake; (3) drying (dewatering) zone - air is sucked through the cake; (4) discharge zone - air pressure loosens the cake and the doctor knife scrapes it off.

Uses: continuous large-scale filtration, e.g. removal of mycelium from fermentation broths in antibiotic production, filtration of calcium carbonate and other high-solid slurries; precoat drum filters handle fine solids.
Merits: continuous and automatic, labour cost low, large capacity, washing and drying in the same cycle, cake thickness controlled by drum speed.
Demerits: costly, complex, only vacuum available so pressure difference is limited (about 1 atmosphere), not suitable for hot or volatile filtrates, cake may crack.
a.diagram: Horizontal drum partly dipped in a slurry trough, rotating clockwise; zones marked around it (filtration, washing with sprays, drying, cake discharge with doctor knife); central rotary valve with vacuum lines to filtrate and wash receivers.
a.conclusion: The rotary drum filter is the standard continuous filter for large volumes of high-solid slurries.

short.q: Write a note on Seitz filter and membrane filters.
short.hi: Seitz: asbestos pad; membrane: 0.22 µm sterilising

kp.t: Seitz: asbestos (and cellulose) pad in metal holder
Seitz removes bacteria by adsorption and sieving; sheds fibres, adsorbs drug
Membrane: thin porous film of cellulose esters, nylon, PTFE
0.22 µm for sterilisation; 0.45 µm for clarification
Membrane works by sieving; clogs easily, needs prefilter

short.a:
Seitz filter: a pad made of asbestos (with cellulose fibres) is held between two metal parts of a holder; liquid is passed under pressure or vacuum. Bacteria are removed by sieving and by adsorption in the pad. Uses: sterilisation of heat-sensitive solutions. Demerits: asbestos fibres may shed into the filtrate, the pad adsorbs drugs (e.g. alkaloids) and may release alkali; single use. It is now largely replaced by membrane filters.
Membrane filters: thin porous films of cellulose esters (acetate, nitrate), nylon, PTFE or PVDF with uniform pore size. They act by sieving (surface filtration). 0.22 µm membranes are used for sterile filtration of injections and ophthalmic solutions; 0.45 µm for clarification and microbial counts.
Merits: no shedding, little adsorption, fast flow, testable (bubble point). Demerits: fragile, clog easily, need a prefilter.

short.q: Name any two materials used for the construction of a pharmaceutical plant.
short.hi: Stainless steel, glass, glass-lined steel, plastics

kp.t: Stainless steel (ferrous)
Glass / glass-lined steel (inorganic non-metal)
Non-ferrous metals / plastics / rubber

short.a:
1. Stainless steel (e.g. SS 304 and SS 316) - used for tanks, mixers, dryers and machine parts that contact the product because it resists corrosion and is easy to clean.
2. Glass and glass-lined steel - used for reaction vessels and pipelines handling corrosive acids.
Others: aluminium, copper, plastics (PVC, PTFE, polypropylene), rubber linings.

short.q: Name any two non-ferrous metals used in pharmaceutical plant construction.
short.hi: Non-ferrous = iron-free: Al, Cu, Pb, Ni

kp.t: Non-ferrous: contain no iron as main constituent
Aluminium
Copper / brass
Lead / nickel / tin / titanium

short.a:
Non-ferrous metals are metals that do not contain iron as the main constituent.
1. Aluminium - light, good heat conductor, resists corrosion due to its oxide film; used for foils, tubes and containers.
2. Copper - excellent thermal conductivity; used in evaporating pans, heat exchanger and condenser tubes.
Others: lead (resists sulphuric acid), nickel, tin, titanium.

short.q: Define corrosion.
short.hi: Corrosion = environment se metal ka dheere dheere kharab hona

kp.t: Gradual destruction / deterioration of metal
By chemical or electrochemical reaction
With its environment (air, moisture, acids)

short.a: Corrosion is the gradual destruction or deterioration of a metal (or material) by chemical or electrochemical reaction with its environment (air, moisture, acids, gases). Example: rusting of iron, forming hydrated ferric oxide (Fe2O3·xH2O).

short.q: What is cathodic protection?
short.hi: Metal ko cathode bana do: sacrificial anode ya impressed current

kp.t: Metal to be protected is made the cathode
Sacrificial anode: more active metal like Zn or Mg
Impressed current from DC source

short.a:
Cathodic protection is a method of preventing corrosion in which the metal to be protected is made the cathode of an electrochemical cell, so it does not corrode.
1. Sacrificial anode method: a more active metal (zinc, magnesium) is connected to it; the active metal corrodes instead.
2. Impressed current method: a direct current from an external source is applied, with an inert anode.
Used for buried pipelines, tanks and ship hulls.

short.q: Name the common material handling equipment used in a pharmaceutical plant.
short.hi: Conveyors, elevators, cranes, forklift, pneumatic transfer

kp.t: Conveyors: belt, screw, roller
Bucket elevator / pneumatic conveying
Cranes, hoists, forklifts, pallet trucks
Pumps and pipes for liquids

short.a:
Material handling is the movement, storage and control of materials in the plant.
Equipment: belt, screw and roller conveyors; bucket elevators; pneumatic (vacuum) conveying systems for powders; cranes and hoists; forklifts, pallet trucks and trolleys; chutes and gravity feeds; pumps and pipelines for liquids; IBCs (bins) for powder transfer.

short.q: Explain different types of corrosion with examples.
short.hi: Uniform, galvanic, pitting, crevice, intergranular, stress

kp.t: Uniform (general) corrosion
Galvanic (bimetallic) corrosion
Pitting corrosion
Crevice / concentration cell (differential aeration)
Intergranular corrosion
Stress corrosion cracking / erosion corrosion

short.a:
1. Uniform (general) corrosion: even attack over the whole surface, e.g. rusting of an iron sheet in moist air; thickness falls uniformly.
2. Galvanic (bimetallic) corrosion: when two different metals are in contact in an electrolyte, the more active metal (anode) corrodes, e.g. steel bolts in a copper plate; zinc-iron.
3. Pitting corrosion: localized attack forming small deep pits, e.g. stainless steel in chloride solutions.
4. Crevice / concentration cell corrosion: in narrow gaps (under gaskets, joints) where oxygen concentration differs (differential aeration); the oxygen-poor area corrodes.
5. Intergranular corrosion: attack along grain boundaries, e.g. stainless steel after improper welding (chromium carbide precipitation).
6. Stress corrosion cracking: cracks due to combined tensile stress and corrosive environment; erosion corrosion: due to fast-flowing fluids or abrasive particles.

short.q: Discuss the factors to be considered in the selection of materials for pharmaceutical plant construction.
short.hi: Chemical, physical, economic factors

kp.t: Chemical: corrosion resistance and no product contamination
Physical: strength, thermal conductivity, ease of fabrication
Ease of cleaning and sterilisation
Economic: cost and maintenance
Thermal expansion / temperature and pressure tolerance

short.a:
1. Chemical factors: the material must not react with or contaminate the product (no leaching of metal ions that may catalyse degradation or cause toxicity); it must resist corrosion by drugs, acids, alkalis, solvents and cleaning agents.
2. Physical factors: mechanical strength, hardness and wear resistance; thermal conductivity (high for heat exchangers, low for insulation); thermal expansion; ease of fabrication, welding and machining; weight.
3. Cleaning and sterilisation: smooth, non-porous surfaces that can be cleaned and steam-sterilised; transparency where inspection is needed (glass).
4. Economic factors: initial cost, life of equipment, maintenance and replacement cost.
5. Operating conditions: temperature, pressure and nature of process.

long.q: Explain the principle, construction, working, uses, merits and demerits of hammer mill and ball mill with neat diagrams.
long.hi: Hammer mill = impact; Ball mill = impact + attrition

kp.t: Hammer mill principle: impact
Hammer mill: swinging hammers on rotor, screen at bottom
Hammer mill: high speed, product size controlled by screen
Ball mill principle: impact and attrition
Ball mill: hollow cylinder with balls rotating on horizontal axis
Critical speed; run at 1/2-3/4 of it
Ball mill: wet and dry grinding, closed system for toxic/sterile
Merits/demerits: hammer mill heat and screen clogging; ball mill slow and noisy

a.intro: Hammer mill and ball mill are commonly used size reduction equipment. The hammer mill works by impact, while the ball mill works by impact and attrition.
points: HAMMER MILL - Principle: impact. Material is hit by rapidly rotating hammers and shattered against the casing.

Construction: a steel casing containing a central shaft (rotor) on which four or more swinging hammers are attached. A screen (sieve) of desired size is fitted at the bottom of the casing. Hammers may be blunt (impact, for brittle material) or knife-edged (cutting, for fibrous material).

Working: the rotor rotates at high speed (about 2500-10000 rpm). Material fed from the top hopper is struck by the hammers and thrown against the casing. It stays in the mill until it is small enough to pass through the screen. Product size depends on rotor speed, screen size and feed rate.
Uses: grinding dried granules, crude drugs, chemicals, wet masses (for granulation) and fibrous material (with knife edge).
Merits: rapid, compact, easy to clean, continuous operation, product size controlled by changing the screen, versatile.
Demerits: heat generated may damage thermolabile drugs, screen may clog with sticky material, wear of hammers and screens causes contamination, not for very hard abrasive materials.
BALL MILL - Principle: impact and attrition. At proper speed the balls are lifted and fall (cascade) on the material (impact), and rub against each other (attrition).

Construction: a hollow cylinder (steel, porcelain or stoneware) rotating on its horizontal axis, about 30-50% filled with balls of steel, porcelain or flint. Material fills the voids between the balls.

Working: at low speed the balls only roll (attrition, little grinding); at too high speed (critical speed) the balls centrifuge with the wall and no grinding occurs. At optimum speed (one-half to three-fourth of critical speed, Nc = 0.5/√(R - r) rps) the balls cascade and give maximum size reduction.
Uses: fine grinding of dyes, pigments, chemicals and crude drugs; wet grinding of suspensions; milling of toxic or sterile materials in a closed cylinder.
Merits: produces very fine powder, wet and dry grinding both possible, closed system (no dust, sterile and toxic material), low installation cost, continuous or batch.
Demerits: slow process, very noisy, wear of balls and cylinder can contaminate product, not suitable for soft, sticky or fibrous materials.
a.diagram: Hammer mill: a casing with a central rotor carrying swinging hammers, feed hopper at top, screen at bottom and product outlet below. Ball mill: horizontal cylinder partly filled with balls, showing three positions of balls - sliding at low speed, cascading at optimum speed, centrifuging at critical speed.
a.conclusion: Hammer mill suits rapid grinding of brittle and fibrous drugs, while ball mill suits fine grinding in a closed system; both are standard pharmaceutical mills.

long.q: Explain the principle, construction and working of venturimeter and orifice meter. Derive the equation for rate of flow and give their merits and demerits.
long.hi: Dono Bernoulli par; venturi me loss kam

kp.t: Principle: Bernoulli's theorem
At constriction velocity increases, pressure decreases
Venturi: converging cone, throat, diverging cone
Orifice: thin plate with sharp-edged hole
Manometer connected upstream and at throat/orifice
Flow equation with coefficient of discharge
Vena contracta in orifice meter
Venturi low pressure loss but costly; orifice cheap but high loss

a.intro: Venturimeter and orifice meter are head (differential pressure) flow meters used to measure the rate of flow of fluid in a pipe. Both work on Bernoulli's theorem.
points: Principle: when a fluid passes through a constriction, its velocity increases and its pressure decreases. The pressure difference between the pipe and the constriction is measured and used to calculate the flow rate.

Venturimeter construction: a short converging cone, a cylindrical throat and a long gradually diverging cone (angle about 5-7 degrees) fitted in the pipe line. Pressure tappings at the upstream section and at the throat are connected to a manometer.

Venturimeter working: as fluid enters the converging part, velocity rises and pressure falls to a minimum at the throat. In the diverging cone velocity falls and most of the pressure is recovered. The manometer reading gives the pressure head difference h.

Derivation: applying Bernoulli's equation between section 1 (pipe) and 2 (throat): P1/ρg + u1²/2g = P2/ρg + u2²/2g. With continuity A1u1 = A2u2, u2 = √(2gh) / √(1 - (A2/A1)²). Flow rate Q = Cd A2 √(2gh) / √(1 - (A2/A1)²).
Coefficient of discharge (Cd): about 0.98 for venturimeter, because losses are very small.

Orifice meter construction: a thin flat plate with a sharp-edged circular hole (orifice) fixed between flanges in the pipe. Pressure taps upstream and just downstream of the plate are connected to a manometer.

Orifice meter working: the jet leaving the orifice contracts to a minimum area called the vena contracta, where velocity is maximum and pressure minimum. The same equation applies, but Cd is about 0.61 because of the sudden contraction and eddies.
Merits of venturimeter: very low permanent pressure loss, high accuracy, suitable for large flows.
Demerits of venturimeter: costly, long, occupies more space, difficult to change for different flow ranges.
Merits of orifice meter: cheap, simple, small, easy to install and replace.
Demerits of orifice meter: large permanent pressure (energy) loss, lower Cd, edge wears with time, not good for slurries.
a.diagram: Venturimeter: pipe with converging cone, throat and diverging cone; U-tube manometer connected between inlet and throat showing level difference h. Orifice meter: pipe with a plate having a central hole, flow lines contracting to vena contracta after the plate, manometer connected across the plate.
a.conclusion: Both meters measure flow rate from a pressure difference; venturimeter is preferred where energy loss matters, orifice meter where low cost and flexibility matter.

long.q: Write the objectives and mechanisms of size separation. Describe the official standards for sieves and powders, and explain the principle, construction and working of a sieve shaker.
long.hi: Sieving: chhote particles mesh se nikal jaate hain

kp.t: Objectives: uniform particle size, quality control
Mechanisms: agitation, brushing, centrifugal
Sieve number definition: meshes per 2.54 cm
Sieves of woven wire, standards for aperture and wire diameter
IP grades of powder: coarse to very fine
Sieve shaker: nest of sieves, coarsest at top
Mechanical shaking/vibration for fixed time, weigh fractions
Merits: simple, cheap; demerits: not for very fine, sticky, clogging

a.intro: Size separation (sieving or classification) is the unit operation in which a mixture of particles is separated into fractions of different sizes. Sieving is the most common method in pharmacy.
points: Objectives: to obtain powders of uniform and desired particle size; to check particle size distribution for quality control; to improve mixing and content uniformity; to remove oversize particles after milling; for granule size control before compression.
Applications: grading of powders for tablets, capsules and dusting powders; particle size analysis; separation of fines from granules.

Mechanisms of sieving: (1) agitation - oscillation, vibration or gyration of the sieve; (2) brushing - a brush moves particles over the mesh and breaks lumps; (3) centrifugal - particles are thrown outward against a cylindrical sieve by a rotating paddle. Particles smaller than the openings pass; larger ones are retained.

Official standards for sieves (IP): sieves are made of woven wire of brass, bronze, stainless steel or other suitable material; wires should be of uniform diameter and not coated. Sieve number = number of meshes in a length of 2.54 cm in each transverse direction. Standards are given for nominal aperture size, wire diameter and tolerance.

Official standards for powders (IP): coarse powder (10/44), moderately coarse (22/60), moderately fine (44/85), fine (85) and very fine (120); the first number is the sieve through which all particles must pass.
Sieve shaker principle: agitation (vibration/shaking) of a nest of sieves separates particles by size.

Construction: a set (nest) of standard sieves stacked one over another with the coarsest at the top and finest at the bottom, a receiving pan below and a lid on top, clamped on a motor-driven shaking device (mechanical or electromagnetic).

Working: a weighed sample is placed on the top sieve. The machine is run for a fixed time (e.g. 10-20 min). Particles move down until retained on a sieve whose openings are smaller than them. Each fraction is weighed and particle size distribution is calculated.
Uses: particle size analysis of powders and granules; quality control.
Merits: simple, cheap, easy to operate, reproducible results.
Demerits: not suitable for very fine particles (below about 40 micron), sieves may get blocked (blinding) with sticky or moist powder, attrition of particles may occur during long shaking.
a.diagram: A vertical stack of sieves (coarsest on top, finest at bottom) with lid and receiver pan, clamped on a vibrating base driven by a motor; arrows showing oscillatory motion.
a.conclusion: Sieve shaker with official sieves is the standard method to grade powders and check particle size distribution as per IP.

long.q: Describe the principle, construction, working, uses, merits and demerits of air separator, bag filter and elutriation tank.
long.hi: Air separator, bag filter, elutriation — fine particle separation

kp.t: Air separator: centrifugal force + air current classify fines
Bag filter: filtration of dust through fabric bags
Bag filter: suction fan, shaking to remove dust
Elutriation: upward fluid stream, settling velocity
Elutriation tank: series of tanks of increasing diameter
Fine particles carried over, coarse settle
Merits/demerits: bag filter very efficient but bags clog/tear; elutriation needs wet/dry later

a.intro: Air separator, bag filter and elutriation tank are size separation equipment used mainly for fine particles where ordinary sieving is not effective.
points: AIR SEPARATOR - Principle: centrifugal force combined with an air current. Fine particles are carried by air, coarse particles fall out.

Construction and working: a cylindrical vessel with a rotating disc and fan blades on a central shaft. Feed falls on the rotating disc and is thrown outward into a rising air stream made by the fan. Fine particles are carried with the air to an outer cone where they settle; coarse particles fall into the inner cone and are removed or returned to the mill.

Uses: removes fines from milled product in a closed circuit with a ball mill or hammer mill. Merits: continuous, used with mill to avoid over-grinding. Demerit: not suitable for very fine separation; power needed.
BAG FILTER - Principle: filtration of dust-laden air through cloth bags; air passes, dust is retained on the inner surface of the bags.

Construction and working: a number of cloth (cotton, wool or synthetic fabric) bags hung inside a metal housing, open at the bottom, connected to an inlet chamber. A fan creates suction, dusty air enters the bags and clean air leaves from the top. Periodically the bags are shaken mechanically (or by reverse air) and the dust falls into a hopper.

Uses: removing fine dust from air in milling and spray drying; with fluidized bed dryers; dust collection in the plant. Merits: very efficient for fine particles, simple. Demerits: bags may tear or clog, not for hot, moist or corrosive gases.

ELUTRIATION TANK - Principle: particles are separated in an upward moving fluid according to their settling velocity (Stokes' law). If the fluid velocity is more than the settling velocity, the particle is carried up; otherwise it settles.

Construction and working: a series of tanks (often three or more) of increasing diameter connected in series. Suspension enters the first (narrowest) tank; as diameter increases, the upward velocity decreases, so progressively finer particles settle in successive tanks and the finest leave with the overflow.

Uses: separating fine powders such as kaolin, chalk and insoluble drugs into size fractions. Merits: separation of very fine particles; continuous. Demerits: product is wet and must be dried; large volume of fluid; material must be insoluble in the liquid.
a.diagram: Air separator: vertical vessel with central rotating disc and fan, inner cone for coarse and outer cone for fines. Bag filter: housing with hanging cloth bags, dusty air inlet at bottom, fan and clean air outlet at top, shaking device and dust hopper. Elutriation: three tanks of increasing diameter in series with arrows of upward flow and overflow.
a.conclusion: These equipment complete size separation for fine powders; bag filter is mainly for dust collection, elutriation for wet classification.

long.q: Explain the principle, construction, working, uses, merits and demerits of fluid energy mill. Add a note on the laws governing size reduction.
long.hi: Jet mill = attrition + impact by high velocity air

kp.t: Principle: attrition and impact by high velocity air jets
Construction: hollow elliptical (loop) pipe with nozzles
Air/inert gas at high pressure; particles collide
Classifier: fines leave at top through outlet
Produces micronized particles (1-30 micron), heat-sensitive drugs
Rittinger, Kick and Bond laws
Demerit: high energy and air cost, dust

a.intro: Fluid energy mill (jet mill or micronizer) is a size reduction equipment that produces very fine (micronized) powders using high velocity air or inert gas instead of moving parts.
points: Principle: size reduction occurs by attrition and impact between particles moving at high velocity in jets of air or inert gas.

Construction: a hollow elliptical (oval loop) pipe of about 20-200 mm diameter and up to about 2 m height. Nozzles for air or inert gas are placed at the bottom; a feed inlet (with venturi feeder) and a classifier outlet are at the top.

Working: air at high pressure enters through the nozzles and moves at very high velocity around the loop. Particles fed in are accelerated, collide with each other and with the wall and are broken. At the top bend, centrifugal force keeps coarse particles circulating, while fine particles leave with the air through the classifier into a cyclone or bag filter.
Uses: to produce particles of about 1-30 micron for aerosols, injections and better dissolution; for heat-sensitive drugs like antibiotics and vitamins.

Merits: very fine and uniform product; no moving parts, so little contamination; expanding gas cools the material, so suitable for thermolabile drugs; can use inert gas for oxygen-sensitive drugs; classification is built in.
Demerits: high energy consumption and cost of compressed air; dust problem; not suitable for soft, sticky or fibrous material; feed must be pre-milled.
Laws of size reduction - Rittinger's law: energy is proportional to the new surface area created, E = KR (1/D2 - 1/D1); applies to fine grinding.
Kick's law: energy is proportional to the size reduction ratio, E = KK ln(D1/D2); applies to coarse crushing.
Bond's law: energy is proportional to (1/√D2 - 1/√D1), using the work index Wi; applies to the intermediate range and is most practical.
a.diagram: An oval (loop) pipe standing vertically; air nozzles at the bottom, feed hopper with venturi on one side, arrows showing particle circulation round the loop, classifier and product outlet at the top leading to a cyclone.
a.conclusion: Fluid energy mill is the choice for micronization of heat-sensitive drugs, and the laws of size reduction help estimate the energy needed for grinding.

long.q: Describe heat transfer mechanisms, Fourier's law, and applications of heat transfer in pharmaceutical operations.
long.hi: Conduction, convection, radiation + Fourier law

kp.t: Conduction: heat flow through solid by molecular vibration, no movement of matter
Fourier's law dQ/dθ = -kA dt/dx
Thermal conductivity k; composite wall resistances in series
Convection: by movement of fluid; natural and forced
Film coefficient h, Q = hAΔt (Newton's law of cooling)
Radiation: electromagnetic waves, no medium; Stefan-Boltzmann σT⁴
Applications: evaporation, distillation, drying, sterilization, crystallization

a.intro: Heat transfer is the flow of heat from a region of higher temperature to a region of lower temperature. In pharmaceutical engineering it occurs by three mechanisms: conduction, convection and radiation.
points: Objectives: to heat or cool materials in a controlled way; to supply latent heat for evaporation, distillation and drying; to maintain temperature in reactions, sterilization and storage.

Conduction: transfer of heat through a body (mainly solids) from molecule to molecule by vibration and free electrons, without any bulk movement of the material, e.g. heat through the wall of a steam-jacketed kettle.

Fourier's law: the rate of heat flow is directly proportional to the area and the temperature gradient: dQ/dθ = -k A dt/dx, where k is thermal conductivity (W/m·K). Metals have high k; insulators (glass wool, asbestos) have low k.
Conduction through a composite wall: for layers in series, Q = Δt / (x1/k1A + x2/k2A + x3/k3A); the total resistance is the sum of individual resistances, like an electric circuit.

Convection: transfer of heat by actual movement of fluid particles. Natural (free) convection is due to density differences caused by temperature; forced convection is caused by a pump, fan or stirrer and is faster.

Heat transfer from fluid to wall: Q = h A Δt, where h is the individual (film) heat transfer coefficient; a stagnant film near the wall gives most resistance. The overall heat transfer coefficient U combines film and wall resistances: 1/U = 1/h1 + x/k + 1/h2.

Radiation: transfer of heat as electromagnetic waves (infrared) without any medium; it can occur in vacuum. A black body absorbs all radiation falling on it. Stefan-Boltzmann law: E = σ T⁴. Kirchhoff's law: at equilibrium emissivity equals absorptivity.

Applications in pharmacy: evaporation of extracts, distillation of solvents and water, drying of granules (tray dryer, fluid bed), sterilization (autoclave, dry heat oven), crystallization, melting of bases for ointments and suppositories, cooling and refrigeration, and heating of reactors.
a.diagram: Three sketches: (1) a slab with hot face T1 and cold face T2 and arrow of heat flow through thickness x (conduction); (2) a vessel heated from below with circulating arrows in the liquid (convection); (3) a hot body sending wavy arrows to a cold body across space (radiation).
a.conclusion: Conduction, convection and radiation usually act together; understanding them helps design evaporators, dryers, heat exchangers and sterilizers.

long.q: What are heat exchangers and heat interchangers? Describe the construction and working of a shell and tube heat exchanger and a double pipe heat exchanger.
long.hi: Shell and tube: tubes me ek fluid, shell me dusra

kp.t: Exchanger: steam/gas to liquid; interchanger: liquid-liquid or gas-gas
Heat transfer through metal wall without mixing
Shell and tube: bundle of tubes in cylindrical shell with tube sheets
Baffles increase velocity/turbulence of shell fluid
Single pass (1-1) and multipass (1-2); floating head for expansion
Double pipe: two concentric pipes
Counter-current flow more efficient than parallel

a.intro: Heat exchangers and interchangers are devices that transfer heat between two fluids separated by a metal wall, so that the fluids do not mix.
points: Heat exchanger: transfers heat from one fluid (hot gas or steam) to another fluid (liquid) through a metal wall, e.g. steam heating a liquid.
Heat interchanger: transfers heat from one liquid to another liquid, or from one gas to another gas, through a metal wall, e.g. hot outgoing product warming the cold feed (heat recovery).

Shell and tube heat exchanger - construction: a bundle of parallel tubes fixed at both ends into tube sheets and enclosed in a cylindrical shell. Headers (channels) at each end distribute the tube-side fluid. Baffles inside the shell direct the shell-side fluid across the tubes.

Working: one fluid (e.g. liquid to be heated) flows through the tubes, the other (e.g. steam) flows in the shell around the tubes; heat passes through the tube walls. Baffles increase velocity and turbulence of the shell fluid and so improve the heat transfer coefficient.

Types: single pass (1-1) exchanger, where the tube fluid passes once; multipass (1-2) exchanger, where partitions in the header make the tube fluid travel twice, giving higher velocity and better heat transfer. A floating head design allows for thermal expansion of tubes.
Merits of shell and tube: large heat transfer area in small space, suitable for high pressures, easy to clean tube side. Demerits: costly, shell side difficult to clean.

Double pipe heat exchanger - construction: two concentric pipes; one fluid flows through the inner pipe and the other through the annular space between the pipes. Several units can be connected in series as hairpins.
Working: usually counter-current flow is used (fluids move in opposite directions), giving a higher mean temperature difference and better heat transfer than parallel (co-current) flow.
Merits of double pipe: simple, cheap, easy to clean and extend. Demerits: small heat transfer area, suitable only for small duties.
Uses in pharmacy: heating and cooling of liquids, condensers in distillation and evaporation, heat recovery, preheating feed of evaporators.
a.diagram: Shell and tube: horizontal cylindrical shell with tube bundle, tube sheets at both ends, baffles alternating top and bottom, inlet and outlet nozzles for shell fluid and tube fluid. Double pipe: inner pipe within outer pipe with arrows showing counter-current flow.
a.conclusion: Shell and tube exchangers are the workhorse for large duties, while double pipe exchangers suit small duties; both work by conduction through a wall with convection on both sides.

long.q: Explain the principle, construction, working, uses, merits and demerits of horizontal tube evaporator and forced circulation evaporator.
long.hi: Horizontal tube: steam tubes ke andar; forced circulation: pump

kp.t: Horizontal tube: steam inside horizontal tubes, liquid outside
Natural circulation, cheap, for non-viscous liquids
Demerits: scaling, poor for viscous/foaming liquids
Forced circulation: pump circulates liquid at high velocity
Boiling suppressed in tubes, flashes in separator
Suitable for viscous, scaling, crystallizing, thermolabile liquids
Demerits of forced: costly pump, power, maintenance

a.intro: Evaporators concentrate solutions by boiling off solvent. The horizontal tube evaporator is a simple natural circulation type, while the forced circulation evaporator uses a pump to move the liquid rapidly over the heating surface.
points: HORIZONTAL TUBE EVAPORATOR - Principle: steam condensing inside horizontal tubes gives latent heat to the liquid outside the tubes, which boils by natural circulation.

Construction: a vertical cylindrical body (cast iron or steel) with a steam compartment at the bottom containing a bundle of horizontal tubes; steam inlet, condensate outlet and vent; feed inlet, product outlet at the bottom and vapour outlet at the top.
Working: liquid is fed to cover the tubes; steam enters the tubes and condenses; the liquid boils and vapour leaves at the top to a condenser; concentrated liquid is withdrawn from the bottom.
Uses: concentration of non-viscous liquids that do not form scale.
Merits: cheap, simple, small headroom, easy to clean the inside of tubes.
Demerits: poor liquid circulation, so low heat transfer; not suitable for viscous, foaming or scale-forming liquids; scale outside tubes is difficult to remove.

FORCED CIRCULATION EVAPORATOR - Principle: a pump forces the liquid at high velocity through a tube heat exchanger (calandria); the liquid is kept under hydrostatic head so it does not boil in the tubes, and it flashes into vapour when it enters the separator.

Construction: a short tube heat exchanger (vertical or horizontal tubes) heated by steam, a vapour-liquid separator (vapour head) with deflector, and a circulating pump connecting the separator back to the heater; feed inlet and product outlet.

Working: liquid is pumped through the tubes at high velocity, gets superheated, then partly flashes in the separator; vapour goes to the condenser and the liquid is recirculated; concentrate is drawn off.
Uses: concentration of viscous liquids, liquors that form scale or crystals, and thermolabile products (high velocity gives short contact and less burning on tubes), e.g. insulin and liver extracts.
Merits: high heat transfer coefficient, less scaling and fouling, suitable for viscous and crystallizing liquids.
Demerits: high cost of pump and power, more maintenance, risk of leaks at pump seal; liquid retention time can be long if recirculated many times.
a.diagram: Horizontal tube: vertical body with horizontal steam tubes near the bottom, steam in/condensate out, feed in, concentrate out, vapour out at top. Forced circulation: heater (calandria), pipe to separator, pump returning liquid from separator to heater, vapour outlet at top of separator.
a.conclusion: Horizontal tube evaporators are cheap for simple liquids, while forced circulation evaporators handle difficult viscous and scaling liquids.

long.q: Explain the principle, construction and working of a multiple effect evaporator. Discuss methods of feeding and the economy of multiple effect evaporator.
long.hi: Ek effect ki vapour agle effect ko garam karti hai

kp.t: Principle: vapour of one effect is heating medium for next
Effects at successively lower pressure / boiling point
Steam only to first effect; last effect to condenser/vacuum
Forward feed
Backward feed
Mixed and parallel feed
Economy = kg vapour per kg steam; increases with number of effects
Capacity not increased; higher cost with more effects

a.intro: A multiple effect evaporator is a set of evaporators (effects) connected in series so that the vapour from one effect is used as the heating steam for the next effect. It saves steam (improves economy).
points: Principle: a liquid boils at a lower temperature when the pressure is reduced. Each effect is kept at a lower pressure than the previous one, so the vapour produced in one effect (at higher temperature) can boil the liquid in the next effect.

Construction: two or more evaporator bodies (e.g. three effects) connected in series by vapour lines. Live steam is supplied only to the first effect. The last effect is connected to a condenser and vacuum pump. Each effect has feed, product and condensate lines.

Working: steam heats the liquid in effect 1; vapour from effect 1 goes to the steam chest of effect 2, which is at lower pressure; vapour of effect 2 heats effect 3, and so on. The vapour from the last effect is condensed. The liquid gets more concentrated from effect to effect.
