Forward feed: feed enters the first effect and flows in the same direction as steam/vapour, to the last effect. No pump needed between effects (pressure falls); suitable for hot feed and thermolabile concentrates since the most concentrated liquid is at the lowest temperature.

Backward feed: feed enters the last (coldest) effect and moves towards the first effect; pumps are needed. Suitable for cold feed and viscous concentrates, because the most concentrated liquid is at the highest temperature where viscosity is lower.
Mixed feed: combination of forward and backward feeding. Parallel feed: fresh feed is given to each effect separately and product withdrawn from each (used in crystallizing evaporators).
Economy: kg of water evaporated per kg of steam supplied. A single effect has economy a little less than 1; with n effects economy increases roughly n times (less in practice due to losses).

Capacity: total evaporation per hour is about the same as a single effect with the same total temperature difference and area, because the temperature difference is divided among effects. So multiple effects improve economy, not capacity.
Merits: large saving of steam (fuel), suitable for large-scale continuous concentration.
Demerits: high installation cost, more complex to operate; the number of effects is limited by cost and the available temperature difference.
a.diagram: Three evaporator bodies in a row: live steam into effect 1, vapour line from top of effect 1 to steam chest of effect 2, effect 2 to effect 3, effect 3 vapour to condenser and vacuum pump; arrows of liquid flow from effect 1 to 3 (forward feed) with pressure P1 > P2 > P3.
a.conclusion: Multiple effect evaporation is the standard method to concentrate large volumes economically; the best number of effects balances steam saving against equipment cost.

long.q: Explain the principle and methodology of distillation under reduced pressure and molecular distillation, with their applications, merits and demerits.
long.hi: Vacuum se boiling point kam; molecular = short path

kp.t: Reduced pressure lowers boiling point
For thermolabile / high boiling substances
Apparatus: Claisen flask, capillary/ebullition tube to prevent bumping, vacuum pump
Molecular: very high vacuum, gap less than mean free path
Molecules reach condenser without collision
Falling film / centrifugal molecular still
Applications: vitamin A from fish liver oil, concentration of extracts

a.intro: Many pharmaceutical substances decompose at their normal boiling points. Distillation under reduced pressure and molecular distillation allow distillation at much lower temperatures.
points: Distillation under reduced pressure - principle: a liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the external pressure. If the pressure above the liquid is reduced by a vacuum pump, the liquid boils at a lower temperature.

Methodology: a Claisen flask (two necks) is used; one neck holds a fine capillary (ebullition) tube that lets a stream of tiny air bubbles in to prevent bumping, the other holds a thermometer. The flask is connected through a condenser to a receiver, a manometer and a vacuum pump. Heating is done on a water/oil bath.

Applications: concentration of extracts with thermolabile constituents (enzymes, vitamins, hormones); distillation of high-boiling liquids that decompose at normal boiling point; solvent recovery at low temperature.
Merits: low temperature protects heat-sensitive drugs; faster distillation. Demerits: bumping and foaming, need for vacuum equipment and leak-proof joints.

Molecular distillation - principle: under very high vacuum (about 10⁻³ mm Hg or less) the distance between the evaporating surface and the condensing surface is made shorter than the mean free path of the molecules, so molecules escaping from the liquid reach the condenser without colliding with gas molecules.

Methodology: the liquid is spread as a thin film on a heated surface - falling film still (liquid flows down a heated vertical wall) or centrifugal still (liquid spread on a rapidly rotating heated cone). A cooled condenser surface is kept very close to it. Distillate and residue are collected separately.
Applications: purification of vitamin A from fish liver oils, separation of vitamins E and other heat-sensitive high molecular weight substances, refining of oils.
Merits: very short exposure to heat, very low temperatures, suitable for high molecular weight and heat-sensitive compounds.
Demerits: expensive equipment, high vacuum needed, low throughput, poor separation of components with similar molecular weight.
a.diagram: Reduced pressure: Claisen flask on water bath with capillary tube and thermometer, condenser, receiver (adapter) connected to manometer and vacuum pump. Molecular still: heated surface with thin liquid film and a closely placed cold condenser surface with high vacuum line.
a.conclusion: Both methods are used for heat-sensitive drugs; molecular distillation is the extreme form used for very high boiling, delicate compounds.

long.q: Explain the mechanisms of mixing for solids, liquids and semi-solids. Add a note on objectives and factors affecting mixing.
long.hi: Solid: convective, shear, diffusive; liquid: bulk, turbulent, laminar, diffusion

kp.t: Objectives: uniform distribution, content uniformity, reaction
Solid mixing: convective mixing
Solid mixing: shear mixing
Solid mixing: diffusive mixing
Liquid mixing: bulk transport, turbulent, laminar, molecular diffusion
Semi-solid mixing: kneading, shearing, folding
Factors: particle size, shape, density, proportion, time
Segregation (demixing) problem

a.intro: Mixing is a unit operation in which two or more components are combined so that each particle of one component lies as nearly as possible next to a particle of the other, giving a uniform product. Mechanisms differ for solids, liquids and semi-solids.
points: Objectives and applications: uniform distribution of drug for content uniformity in tablets, capsules and powders; preparation of granules, emulsions, suspensions, ointments and creams; promotion of heat and mass transfer and chemical reactions.
Solid mixing - convective mixing: transfer of groups (lumps) of particles from one location to another by blades, paddles or tumbling (macro-mixing), e.g. ribbon blender.
Solid mixing - shear mixing: forces of attrition produce slip planes within the powder bed; layers move over each other and mix, e.g. sigma blade and planetary mixers.
Solid mixing - diffusive mixing: random movement of individual particles over freshly formed surfaces, as in tumbling mixers (double cone, V-blender); it gives micro-mixing.
Liquid mixing - bulk transport: movement of large portions of liquid from one place to another by the impeller (convection).
Liquid mixing - turbulent mixing: random high-velocity eddies created at high Reynolds number break up the liquid into small portions.
Liquid mixing - laminar mixing: in viscous liquids, layers are stretched and sheared, decreasing striation thickness; molecular diffusion completes mixing at the smallest scale.
Semi-solid mixing: semisolids do not flow freely; mixing occurs by kneading, shearing, folding and smearing of the mass against the vessel wall (sigma blade, planetary mixer, triple roller mill).

Difference between solid and liquid mixing: liquid mixing is helped by turbulence and molecular diffusion and is easy to make uniform; solid mixing depends on movement of particles, cannot become perfect and is prone to segregation.

Factors affecting mixing: particle size and size distribution, particle shape, density difference, proportion of components, surface charge and cohesiveness, moisture, viscosity (liquids), mixer type, speed, fill volume and mixing time.

Segregation (demixing): differences in particle size, density and shape cause particles to separate during mixing, transport or storage (percolation, trajectory, elutriation); it is reduced by matching particle size and density and by avoiding over-mixing.
a.diagram: Three small diagrams: (1) powder bed with arrows showing group movement (convective), slip planes (shear) and single particles moving (diffusive); (2) tank with impeller and eddies for liquid mixing; (3) mass being folded and kneaded by blades for semisolids.
a.conclusion: Choosing the right mechanism and mixer for solids, liquids or semisolids gives uniform products and avoids segregation.

long.q: Explain the principle, construction, working, uses, merits and demerits of fluidized bed dryer with a neat diagram.
long.hi: Hot air neeche se, granules hawa me float karke dry

kp.t: Principle: hot air through bed fluidises particles
Each particle surrounded by hot air - high heat & mass transfer
Bowl with perforated (mesh) bottom
Fan, heater, bag filters at top
Drying time short; uniform temperature
Uses: tablet granules, also granulation and coating
Demerits: static electricity / explosion risk, fines (attrition), not for sticky

a.intro: A fluidized bed dryer (FBD) dries wet solid particles (mainly granules) by suspending them in an upward stream of hot air, so each particle is surrounded by drying gas.
points: Principle: when hot air is passed upward through a bed of particles at a velocity greater than the settling velocity of the particles, the bed becomes fluidized (particles are partially suspended and behave like a boiling liquid). Each particle is completely surrounded by hot air, giving very high heat and mass transfer and rapid drying.

Construction: a stainless steel product container (bowl) with a perforated or wire-mesh bottom, mounted on a trolley; an air inlet with filter and heater below; a fan at the top that draws air through the bed; bag (finger) filters above the bowl to retain fines; a shaker to clean the bags; temperature controls.

Working: wet granules are loaded in the bowl and placed in the dryer. Fresh air is filtered, heated and drawn upward through the bed by the fan. Granules are lifted and fluidized and dry quickly. Moist air leaves through the bag filters. After drying, the bowl is removed and unloaded.
Drying time is short (minutes instead of hours in a tray dryer) and the temperature of the bed is uniform.
Uses: drying of tablet granules; the same equipment (fluid bed processor) is used for granulation and coating of particles.
Merits: rapid drying, uniform temperature, high output per unit area, easy loading and unloading, granules remain free (no lumps), can be automated.

Demerits: fine particles and organic solvent vapours may cause static charge and dust explosion (earthing needed), attrition of granules produces fines, not suitable for sticky or toxic materials, bags need cleaning.
a.diagram: Vertical cabinet: bowl with perforated bottom on trolley in the middle, fluidized granules shown as dots with upward arrows, air inlet with filter and heater at bottom, bag filters above the bowl, fan and exhaust at the top.
a.conclusion: Fluidized bed drying is the standard modern method for drying tablet granules because it is fast and uniform.

long.q: Explain the principle, construction and working of a freeze dryer. Discuss the stages of freeze drying, its applications, merits and demerits.
long.hi: Freeze drying = sublimation of ice under vacuum

kp.t: Principle: sublimation of ice under vacuum
Below triple point of water (0.0098 °C, 4.58 mm Hg)
Freezing below eutectic temperature
Primary drying: sublimation of ice
Secondary drying: removal of bound water (desorption)
Equipment: drying chamber with shelves, condenser, vacuum pump, heater
Applications: antibiotics, vaccines, plasma, proteins
Demerits: costly, long process

a.intro: Freeze drying (lyophilisation) is a drying process in which water is removed from a frozen product by sublimation (ice directly to vapour) under vacuum. It is used for drugs that are damaged by heat or water.
points: Principle: below the triple point of water (0.0098 °C and 4.58 mm Hg), ice changes directly into vapour without melting when heat is supplied. In freeze drying the product is frozen and then dried under vacuum so that ice sublimes.

Construction: (1) drying chamber with temperature-controlled hollow shelves (heated or cooled) for vials/trays; (2) vapour condenser kept at very low temperature (about -40 to -60 °C) to trap vapour as ice; (3) vacuum pump; (4) refrigeration and heating systems; (5) controls for pressure and temperature.

Stage 1 - Preparation and freezing: the solution is filled in vials (partly stoppered) or trays and frozen on the shelves (or shell-frozen) below its eutectic temperature so that all water becomes ice.

Stage 2 - Primary drying: vacuum is applied and a small, controlled amount of heat is supplied through the shelves; ice sublimes and vapour travels to the condenser. Most (frozen, unbound) water is removed. The temperature must stay below the collapse/eutectic temperature.
Stage 3 - Secondary drying: the shelf temperature is raised (still under vacuum) to remove the remaining bound (adsorbed) water by desorption, to a very low final moisture content.
Stage 4 - Packing: vials are stoppered inside the chamber (under vacuum or nitrogen) and sealed.
Applications: dry powder injections of antibiotics, vaccines, sera, blood plasma, proteins, enzymes, hormones and microbial cultures; some diagnostic products.
Merits: drying at low temperature, so thermolabile drugs are protected; porous product reconstitutes rapidly; little loss of volatile constituents; aseptic handling possible; long shelf life.
Demerits: very expensive equipment and running cost; long process (often a day or more); product is hygroscopic and needs moisture-proof packing; needs skilled operation.
a.diagram: Phase diagram of water showing triple point and sublimation path below it; plus equipment sketch: drying chamber with shelves holding vials, connected to a cold condenser and vacuum pump, with refrigeration and heating lines.
a.conclusion: Freeze drying is the best method for heat-sensitive biologicals and injections, though it is costly and slow.

long.q: Explain the mechanism of drying and the rate of drying curve. Add a note on the measurement and applications of equilibrium moisture content.
long.hi: Drying = heat transfer + mass transfer; constant aur falling rate

kp.t: Drying: removal of liquid by evaporation to give solid
Simultaneous heat and mass transfer
Initial adjustment period
Constant rate period: surface saturated, unbound water
Critical moisture content
First and second falling rate periods (diffusion/capillary)
EMC measured by exposing to known RH (saturated salt solutions) until constant weight
EMC applications: storage, packaging, drying end point

a.intro: Drying is the removal of a liquid (usually water) from a solid or semisolid material by evaporation, to reduce the moisture content to an acceptably low value. It involves simultaneous heat transfer (to evaporate the liquid) and mass transfer (moisture moving to the surface and into the air).
points: Objectives and applications: improve stability of drugs, ease of handling and processing (granules for compression), reduce weight for transport, prevent microbial growth, preparation of dry extracts and powders.

Mechanism: heat is supplied to the wet solid by convection, conduction or radiation; water evaporates from the surface into the air; internal moisture moves to the surface by capillary action and diffusion. The rate depends on air temperature, humidity, velocity and on the nature of the solid.
Rate of drying curve: a plot of drying rate against moisture content (or time). Segment A-B is the initial adjustment period, when the solid warms up (or cools) to the drying temperature.

Constant rate period (B-C): the surface remains saturated with water (unbound moisture), so water evaporates as from a free water surface; rate is constant and controlled by external conditions (air temperature, humidity, velocity).
Critical moisture content (point C): the moisture content at which the constant rate period ends and the surface starts to dry out.
First falling rate period (C-D): unsaturated surface drying; dry patches appear and the wetted surface area decreases, so rate falls.

Second falling rate period (D-E): the rate is controlled by movement of moisture from the interior to the surface by diffusion and capillary flow; it continues until the equilibrium moisture content is reached.
Equilibrium moisture content (EMC): moisture content of a solid in equilibrium with air of given temperature and relative humidity; below it the solid cannot be dried under those conditions.

Measurement of EMC: samples of the material are kept in closed chambers (desiccators) over saturated salt solutions that maintain known relative humidities at constant temperature; the samples are weighed periodically until constant weight, and moisture content is calculated. A plot of EMC vs RH (sorption isotherm) is drawn.

Applications of EMC: deciding storage conditions and packaging for hygroscopic drugs, selecting drying end point and conditions, predicting moisture uptake by granules and tablets, and stability studies.
a.diagram: Graph with drying rate on Y-axis and moisture content on X-axis: horizontal line B-C (constant rate), C marked critical moisture content, falling curve C-D (first falling rate) and D-E (second falling rate) to EMC; initial segment A-B.
a.conclusion: The rate of drying curve explains why drying slows down near the end and helps choose dryers and drying conditions; EMC sets the lowest attainable moisture.

long.q: Describe the construction and working of propellers, turbines and paddles used for liquid mixing. Give their merits and demerits and how vortex formation is prevented.
long.hi: Propeller axial, turbine radial, paddle slow viscous

kp.t: Propeller: high speed, axial flow, low viscosity liquids
Turbine: flat/curved blades on disc, radial flow
Turbine handles wider viscosity range, high shear
Paddle: large flat blades, low speed, tangential flow
Paddle for viscous liquids, poor vertical mixing
Vortex prevented by baffles, off-centre or angled mounting

a.intro: Liquid mixing in tanks is done by rotating impellers. The three main types are propellers, turbines and paddles; they differ in shape, speed and the flow pattern they produce.
points: Flow patterns: axial (parallel to the shaft), radial (perpendicular to the shaft, towards the wall) and tangential (circular, round the shaft). Tangential flow causes vortex formation and poor mixing.

Propeller - construction: two to four inclined (pitched) blades like a ship's propeller fixed to a shaft; small diameter compared with the tank; runs at high speed (several hundred to a few thousand rpm).
Propeller - working and uses: produces mainly axial flow, moving the liquid up and down the tank; suitable for low-viscosity liquids, dissolving solids and preparing solutions and dilute suspensions.
Propeller - merits/demerits: efficient for large volumes of thin liquids, cheap; not effective for viscous liquids; vortex forms if mounted centrally without baffles.
Turbine - construction: several flat, curved or inclined blades attached to a central disc or hub, with diameter larger than a propeller; runs at moderate speed.
Turbine - working and uses: produces radial (and tangential) flow with high shear near the blades; suitable for a wider range of viscosities, emulsions, gas dispersion and suspensions.
Turbine - merits/demerits: effective mixing of medium-viscosity liquids and good shear; costlier and needs more power; baffles needed to prevent swirling.
Paddle - construction: two or four large flat blades on a vertical shaft, diameter about half to most of the tank; runs at low speed (low rpm); anchor and gate paddles scrape the wall.
Paddle - working and uses: mainly tangential and radial flow; used for viscous liquids, pastes, and to prevent sticking on heated walls (anchor type).
Paddle - merits/demerits: simple, low speed, good for viscous materials; poor vertical (axial) mixing, vortex formation, not for low-viscosity rapid mixing.

Prevention of vortex: fitting baffles (vertical strips on the tank wall), mounting the impeller off-centre or at an angle, or using a side-entering impeller; these convert swirl into useful axial/radial flow.
a.diagram: Three sketches in a tank: propeller with arrows going up and down along the shaft (axial), turbine with arrows going outward to the wall and splitting (radial), paddle with wide blades and circular arrows; a baffled tank showing vertical strips on the wall.
a.conclusion: Propellers suit thin liquids, turbines a broad range, and paddles viscous materials; baffles are used to avoid vortex and improve mixing.

long.q: Define filtration. Discuss the theories of filtration and the factors influencing filtration. Add a note on filter aids and filter media.
long.hi: Poiseuille, Darcy, Kozeny-Carman; area, pressure, viscosity

kp.t: Filtration: separation of solids from fluid through porous medium
Mechanisms: straining, impingement, entanglement, attraction
Poiseuille's equation (capillary flow)
Darcy's law
Kozeny-Carman equation (porosity, surface area)
Factors: area, pressure difference, viscosity, cake thickness, particle size, temperature
Filter aids: kieselguhr, perlite; precoat / body mix
Filter media: cloth, paper, metal, sintered, membrane

a.intro: Filtration is the process of separating solid particles from a fluid (liquid or gas) by passing the fluid through a porous medium (filter medium) that retains the solids. The clear liquid is the filtrate and the retained solid is the cake.
points: Objectives and applications: clarification of liquids (syrups, elixirs, injections), sterilisation of heat-sensitive solutions, collection of solids (crystals, precipitates), removal of mycelium from fermentation broth, air filtration in aseptic areas, water treatment.
Mechanisms of retention: straining (particles larger than pores are stopped), impingement (particles hit the fibres due to inertia), entanglement in the fibrous mass, and electrostatic attraction.

Poiseuille's equation: the filter bed is considered a set of capillaries. dV/dt = π r⁴ ΔP / (8 η L); flow rate depends strongly on pore radius (fourth power), pressure difference, viscosity and length of capillary.
Darcy's law: dV/dt = K A ΔP / (η L), where K is the permeability of the bed; rate is proportional to area and pressure difference and inversely proportional to viscosity and bed thickness.

Kozeny-Carman equation: dV/dt = A ΔP ε³ / [K η L S² (1 - ε)²], where ε = porosity of the bed and S = specific surface area of particles (K is the Kozeny constant, about 5). It shows the large effect of cake porosity and particle size.

Factors influencing filtration: (1) area of filter surface - more area, faster; (2) pressure difference - higher pressure increases rate (unless cake is compressible); (3) viscosity of filtrate - lower viscosity (higher temperature) increases rate; (4) thickness of cake - rate falls as cake builds; (5) particle size and porosity of cake - fine or slimy particles reduce rate; (6) compressibility of cake; (7) nature of filter medium and pore size.

Filter aids: inert, insoluble, porous materials (diatomaceous earth/kieselguhr, perlite, cellulose, asbestos, charcoal, talc) that form a porous cake and prevent fine or gelatinous solids blocking the medium. Used as a precoat on the medium or mixed with the slurry (body mix). Requirements: chemically inert, insoluble, low density, porous, free from impurities.

Filter media: woven cloth (cotton, nylon, terylene), filter paper, felt, metal mesh and perforated sheets, metafilter rings, sintered glass and metal, porcelain, asbestos pads and membrane filters. A good medium retains solids, allows high flow, is strong and inert, does not shed fibres and is easy to clean or replace.
a.conclusion: Filtration rate is governed by area, pressure difference, viscosity and cake resistance as shown by the theories; filter aids and correct filter media keep the rate high and the filtrate clear.

long.q: Explain the principle, construction, working, uses, merits and demerits of plate and frame filter press with a neat diagram.
long.hi: Plates aur frames alternate; frame me cake jama hota hai

kp.t: Principle: pressure filtration through cloth
Alternate plates and frames assembled on rails
Frame hollow, collects cake; plate grooved, drains filtrate
Slurry enters frames through channel; filtrate through cloth to plate outlet
Washing: thorough washing with wash plates (buttons 1-2-3)
Uses: collecting solids, sterile filtration with pads
Merits: large area, compact, versatile
Demerits: batch, labour intensive, leakage, cloth wear

a.intro: The plate and frame filter press is a batch pressure filter that gives a large filtering area in a small space. Slurry is pumped under pressure and the solids collect as cake in the frames.
points: Principle: filtration under pressure. The slurry is forced through filter cloth; solids are retained in the frames and filtrate flows through the cloth and along the grooved plate surfaces to the outlet.
Construction - plates: square plates with ridged or grooved surfaces (to support the cloth and drain filtrate) and a filtrate outlet; covered on both sides by filter cloth.
Construction - frames: open (hollow) square frames with a slurry inlet channel; the space inside the frame holds the cake. Frame thickness decides the cake capacity.

Assembly: plates and frames are arranged alternately (plate-frame-plate...) on horizontal rails between a fixed head and a movable end, with cloths between them, and pressed tightly by a screw or hydraulic ram. Holes in the corners line up to form continuous channels for slurry, filtrate and wash water.

Working: slurry is pumped into the channel and enters each frame; liquid passes through the cloths on both sides, runs down the grooves of the plates and leaves through outlets; solids build up in frames until they are full or the rate falls too low.

Washing: in thorough washing, special washing plates are used (plates, frames and wash plates are marked with one, two and three buttons); wash water enters the washing plates, passes through the whole cake and leaves through the outlets of the plain plates.
Discharge: the press is opened, frames are emptied, cloths cleaned or changed and the press reassembled.
Uses: collection of solids (precipitates, crystals), clarification of liquids, sterile filtration using sheets/pads, filtration of viscous liquids under pressure.
Merits: large filtering area per floor space, construction is simple, can work at high pressure, number of plates can be changed, cake can be washed and is fairly dry, no moving parts.
Demerits: batch process, labour intensive dismantling and cleaning, leakage between plates, filter cloths wear quickly, not economical for large amounts of solids, time lost in opening and closing.
a.diagram: Side view: alternate plates (with grooved faces) and frames (hollow) clamped between fixed head and movable end on rails; filter cloth between each; arrows showing slurry entering frames through a top channel, filtrate passing through cloth, running down plate grooves to outlet taps; close-up of one plate and frame showing buttons.
a.conclusion: The plate and frame press is a versatile, low-cost pressure filter for batch work, especially when solids must be collected or sterile pads used.

long.q: Discuss the principle and applications of centrifugation. Describe the principle, construction, working, uses, merits and demerits of super centrifuge and semi-continuous centrifuge.
long.hi: Centrifugal force = gravity se kai guna, separation fast

kp.t: Principle: centrifugal force many times gravity speeds separation
Stokes' law with g replaced by ω²r
Applications: separation of crystals, immiscible liquids, clarification, blood
Super centrifuge: long narrow tubular bowl at very high speed
Two liquid layers leave through separate outlets
Semi-continuous (peeler): horizontal basket, knife removes cake at full speed
Demerits: super - small capacity; semi-continuous - crystal breakage, costly

a.intro: Centrifugation is a unit operation in which a mixture is separated by applying centrifugal force produced by rapid rotation. It is used for separating solids from liquids and immiscible liquids of different densities.
points: Principle: a particle rotating at radius r with angular velocity ω experiences a centrifugal force mω²r, which can be thousands of times the force of gravity. Settling velocity by Stokes' law becomes u = d²(ρs - ρ)ω²r / 18η, so separation that takes hours under gravity takes minutes. RCF = ω²r/g = 1.118 × 10⁻⁵ r N².

Objectives and applications: separation of crystals from mother liquor; removal of solvent from wet crystals; separation of immiscible liquids and breaking of emulsions; clarification of liquids, oils and syrups; separation of blood cells and plasma; collection of cells and mycelium; evaluation of emulsion and suspension stability; purification of proteins and viruses (ultracentrifuge).
SUPER CENTRIFUGE - Principle: centrifugal sedimentation in a very fast, narrow bowl; separates immiscible liquids into layers and deposits fine solids on the wall.

Construction: a long, narrow tubular bowl of small diameter suspended from a flexible spindle at the top and driven at very high speed (thousands of rpm); feed nozzle at the bottom; two outlets at the top - one for the heavier liquid (outer layer) and one for the lighter liquid (inner layer).

Working: feed enters at the bottom and is spun; the heavier liquid forms the outer layer and the lighter the inner layer; both move up and overflow through their own outlets; solids collect on the wall and are removed by stopping the machine.

Uses: separation of oil and water, breaking emulsions, clarification of oils, fruit juices and syrups, separation of blood fractions. Merits: very high centrifugal force, continuous liquid flow, compact. Demerits: small capacity, solids must be removed manually (batch for solids), costly.

SEMI-CONTINUOUS (PEELER) CENTRIFUGE - Principle: centrifugal filtration in a perforated basket that keeps running at constant speed while loading, washing, spinning and unloading take place automatically in sequence.
Construction: a horizontal perforated basket lined with a filter cloth/screen, a feed pipe, a wash spray, and a hydraulically operated knife (unloader) with a chute.

Working: slurry is fed until the cake reaches a set thickness; the cake is washed and spun dry; then the knife moves into the cake and peels it off into the chute, all at full speed; the cycle repeats.

Uses: large-scale separation of crystals and granular solids from liquids. Merits: no stopping between cycles, high output, automatic, less labour. Demerits: the knife may break crystals, a thin layer of cake remains on the screen, costly and complex.
a.diagram: Super centrifuge: tall narrow tubular bowl hanging from a top drive, feed entering at the bottom, two concentric liquid layers and two outlets at the top. Peeler centrifuge: horizontal perforated basket with feed pipe, cake layer, and knife moving in to discharge cake into a chute.
a.conclusion: Centrifuges multiply gravity to speed up separation; the super centrifuge suits liquid-liquid separation and the peeler centrifuge suits continuous crystal handling.

long.q: Define corrosion. Explain the theories of corrosion and discuss the methods for prevention of corrosion.
long.hi: Dry (chemical) aur wet (electrochemical) theory; coating, cathodic protection

kp.t: Definition: destruction of metal by chemical/electrochemical reaction with environment
Chemical (dry) corrosion by direct reaction with gases
Pilling-Bedworth rule / protective oxide film
Electrochemical (wet) theory: anode and cathode in electrolyte
Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻; hydrogen evolution or oxygen absorption at cathode
Prevention: proper material selection and design
Protective coatings: galvanizing, electroplating, paints, linings
Cathodic protection and inhibitors, environment control

a.intro: Corrosion is the gradual destruction of a metal by chemical or electrochemical reaction with its environment. It causes loss of equipment strength, leakage and contamination of pharmaceutical products with metal ions, so it must be prevented.
points: Chemical (dry) corrosion theory: occurs by direct chemical reaction of the metal with dry gases such as oxygen, chlorine or hydrogen sulphide, usually at high temperatures, e.g. 2Fe + O2 → 2FeO. A layer of corrosion product (oxide) forms on the surface.

Nature of the oxide film decides further attack (Pilling-Bedworth rule): if the oxide volume is equal to or greater than that of the metal, a compact, protective film forms (e.g. Al, Cr) and corrosion stops; if it is smaller, a porous film forms and corrosion continues (e.g. alkali metals).

Electrochemical (wet) theory: occurs when a metal is in contact with moisture or an electrolyte. Small anodic and cathodic areas form on the metal (due to impurities, stress or differences in oxygen concentration), creating galvanic cells.
At the anode the metal dissolves (oxidation): Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻. Electrons flow to the cathode.

At the cathode: in acidic medium hydrogen is evolved, 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H2; in neutral or alkaline aerated medium oxygen is absorbed, O2 + 2H2O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻. Fe²⁺ and OH⁻ combine to form Fe(OH)2, which is oxidised to rust (Fe2O3·xH2O).
Prevention 1 - proper selection of material: use corrosion-resistant materials (stainless steel 316, glass-lined steel, plastics) suited to the chemicals handled; use pure metals or suitable alloys.
Prevention 2 - proper design: avoid contact of dissimilar metals (or insulate them), avoid crevices, sharp corners and stagnant areas, allow complete drainage, prefer welded to riveted joints.

Prevention 3 - protective coatings: metallic coatings (galvanizing with zinc, tinning, electroplating with nickel or chromium); non-metallic coatings (paints, lacquers, enamels, glass lining, rubber and plastic linings); chemical conversion coatings (phosphating); passivation of stainless steel with nitric acid.
Prevention 4 - cathodic protection: making the structure the cathode using sacrificial anodes (zinc, magnesium) or impressed current.

Prevention 5 - modification of environment and inhibitors: removing oxygen (deaeration), reducing humidity, controlling pH, and adding corrosion inhibitors (anodic inhibitors such as chromates and phosphates; cathodic inhibitors) to liquids.
a.diagram: Electrochemical cell on an iron surface: water drop as electrolyte, anodic area in the centre where Fe goes to Fe²⁺ with electrons flowing through metal to cathodic area at the edge where O2 + H2O gives OH⁻; rust deposit shown between them.
a.conclusion: Corrosion is mainly an electrochemical process; it is controlled by correct material and design, protective coatings, cathodic protection and control of the environment.

long.q: Classify materials used for pharmaceutical plant construction. Discuss ferrous metals, non-ferrous metals, and inorganic and organic non-metals with their properties and uses.
long.hi: Metals (ferrous, non-ferrous) + non-metals (inorganic, organic)

kp.t: Classification: metals (ferrous, non-ferrous) and non-metals (inorganic, organic)
Cast iron and carbon (mild) steel
Stainless steel: chromium (≥ about 11-12%) + nickel; 304, 316 (Mo)
Non-ferrous: aluminium, copper, lead, nickel, tin, titanium
Inorganic non-metals: glass, glass-lined steel, ceramics, graphite
Organic non-metals: plastics (PVC, PE, PP, PTFE), rubber, wood
Thermoplastics vs thermosetting plastics
Merits/demerits: glass brittle; plastics weak at high temperature

a.intro: Materials used for pharmaceutical plant construction are classified into metals and non-metals. Metals are ferrous (iron-based) or non-ferrous; non-metals are inorganic (glass, ceramics) or organic (plastics, rubber, wood).
points: Cast iron: iron with about 2-4% carbon; cheap, easily cast, good compressive strength but brittle and corrodes; used for machine bases, frames, pipe fittings and some pumps; not for product contact.

Carbon (mild) steel: low carbon, strong, tough, easily welded and cheap but rusts readily; used for structures, steam lines, jackets and storage tanks for non-corrosive materials, often with protective coatings or linings.

Stainless steel: alloy of iron with chromium (at least about 11-12%), which forms a thin passive chromium oxide film that resists corrosion; nickel improves resistance and ductility. SS 304 (18% Cr, 8% Ni, '18/8') for general equipment; SS 316 (with 2-3% molybdenum) has better resistance to chlorides and pitting and is preferred for product-contact parts of tanks, mixers, dryers and tablet machines. Easy to clean and sterilise; costly.

Non-ferrous metals - aluminium: light, good thermal conductor, resistant to many chemicals due to oxide film, but attacked by alkalis and strong acids; used for foils, collapsible tubes, containers and some equipment.

Copper and brass: very high thermal conductivity; used for evaporating pans, heat exchanger and condenser tubes; attacked by ammonia and acids and copper traces may catalyse drug degradation. Lead: resists sulphuric acid, used for linings, but soft and toxic. Nickel: resists alkalis, used in alloys and plating. Tin: for coating (tinning). Titanium: excellent corrosion resistance, costly.

Inorganic non-metals - glass: borosilicate glass is transparent, chemically inert (except to hydrofluoric acid and hot strong alkalis), smooth and easy to clean; used for pipelines, reaction vessels, condensers and lab apparatus. Demerits: brittle, poor resistance to thermal and mechanical shock.

Glass-lined steel: steel vessel with fused glass lining; combines strength of steel with inertness of glass; used for reactors and storage of corrosive acids. Lining can chip. Ceramics, porcelain and stoneware: inert, resist acids, used for mortars, tanks and filters; brittle. Impervious graphite (carbon): good conductor, resists corrosion, used in heat exchangers.

Organic non-metals - plastics: thermoplastics (soften on heating, can be remoulded) such as PVC, polyethylene, polypropylene, PTFE (Teflon), nylon; thermosetting plastics (set permanently on heating) such as phenol-formaldehyde and epoxy resins. Light, cheap, corrosion resistant, easy to fabricate; used for pipes, tanks, linings, gaskets, containers, filter parts.
Demerits of plastics: low strength and softening at higher temperatures, may absorb drugs or leach additives (plasticisers), some are attacked by organic solvents.

Rubber (natural and synthetic): used for linings of tanks, hoses, gaskets and seals; resists many acids and alkalis but is attacked by oils and solvents (natural rubber). Wood: cheap, used for some tanks and vats in the past; porous and hard to clean, so rarely used in modern GMP plants.
a.conclusion: Stainless steel (especially SS 316) is the main material for product-contact equipment, supported by glass, glass-lined steel and plastics where special corrosion resistance or inertness is needed.

mcq.q: Reynolds number is the ratio of:
mcq.explain: Re = Duρ/μ = inertial force / viscous force; it is dimensionless.

mcq.q: Bernoulli's theorem is based on the law of conservation of:
mcq.explain: Total energy (pressure + kinetic + potential) of an ideal fluid in steady flow remains constant.

mcq.q: The coefficient of discharge of a venturimeter is about:
mcq.explain: Venturimeter has very little loss (Cd ≈ 0.98); an orifice meter has Cd ≈ 0.61 due to vena contracta and eddies.

mcq.q: A rotameter is classified as a:
mcq.explain: The float rises in a tapered tube, so the annular flow area changes with flow rate while pressure drop stays constant.

mcq.q: A Pitot tube measures:
options: Average velocity of fluid in the pipe
mcq.explain: It converts kinetic energy at one point into impact pressure; u = √(2gh) gives the velocity at that point.

mcq.q: Kick's law of size reduction is most applicable to:
mcq.explain: Kick's law (energy ∝ size reduction ratio) fits coarse crushing; Rittinger's law fits fine grinding.

mcq.q: According to Rittinger's law, the energy required for size reduction is proportional to:
mcq.explain: E = KR(1/D2 - 1/D1), i.e. proportional to the new surface created.

mcq.q: For efficient grinding, a ball mill should be operated at:
options: Less than one-tenth of critical speed
About one-half to three-fourth of critical speed
mcq.explain: At critical speed balls centrifuge with the wall; at too low speed they only roll. Cascading at 50-75% of critical speed gives maximum impact.

mcq.q: Micronization of a heat-sensitive antibiotic is best done using a:
mcq.explain: Fluid energy (jet) mill gives 1-30 µm particles and the expanding air cools the material, protecting thermolabile drugs.

mcq.q: Sieve number indicates the number of meshes in a length of:
mcq.explain: Sieve number = number of meshes in 2.54 cm (one inch) in each transverse direction.

mcq.q: As per IP, a 'very fine powder' is one in which all particles pass through sieve number:
mcq.explain: IP grades: coarse 10/44, moderately coarse 22/60, moderately fine 44/85, fine 85, very fine 120.

mcq.q: Separation of particles in an elutriation tank is based on:
options: Settling velocity in an upward moving fluid
mcq.explain: Particles whose Stokes settling velocity is lower than the upward fluid velocity are carried over; larger ones settle.

mcq.q: Fourier's law is the basic law of heat transfer by:
mcq.explain: dQ/dθ = -kA dt/dx describes conduction through a solid.

mcq.q: According to the Stefan-Boltzmann law, energy radiated by a black body is proportional to:
mcq.explain: E = σT⁴, where T is absolute temperature.

mcq.q: Heat transfer between two liquids through a metal wall is carried out in a:
mcq.explain: Heat interchangers transfer heat liquid-to-liquid or gas-to-gas; heat exchangers transfer from steam/hot gas to a liquid.

mcq.q: Economy of an evaporator is defined as:
options: Kg of steam used per hour
Heat transfer area per kg of feed
Kg of water evaporated per kg of steam supplied
mcq.explain: Economy = kg vapour produced / kg steam fed.

mcq.q: Increasing the number of effects in a multiple effect evaporator mainly increases:
mcq.explain: Each effect reuses the vapour of the previous one, improving steam economy; total capacity remains about the same.

mcq.q: Backward feeding in a multiple effect evaporator is preferred when:
options: Feed is hot and concentrate is thermolabile
Feed is cold and the concentrate is viscous
mcq.explain: In backward feed the most concentrated (viscous) liquid is in the hottest first effect, where viscosity is lowest.

mcq.q: Climbing film evaporator is especially suitable for:
mcq.explain: Thin film and short residence time protect heat-sensitive drugs; high vapour velocity breaks foam.

mcq.q: Forced circulation evaporator is the best choice for:
options: Very small volumes of thin liquids
mcq.explain: A pump drives liquid at high velocity; boiling is suppressed in tubes, reducing scaling and fouling.

mcq.q: Steam distillation is based on the principle that:
options: Immiscible liquids boil when the sum of their vapour pressures equals atmospheric pressure
Molecules travel less than mean free path
mcq.explain: Each immiscible liquid exerts its own vapour pressure, so the mixture boils below 100 °C.

mcq.q: In molecular distillation, the distance between evaporating and condensing surfaces is kept:
options: Less than the mean free path of molecules
mcq.explain: Under high vacuum, molecules reach the condenser without collisions.

mcq.q: Flash distillation is also known as:
mcq.explain: Vapour and liquid formed by sudden pressure release are in equilibrium and are separated.

mcq.q: During the constant rate period of drying, the surface of the solid is:
mcq.explain: Unbound water keeps the surface saturated, so evaporation is like from a free water surface.

mcq.q: Critical moisture content is the moisture content at which:
options: The constant rate period ends and falling rate begins
mcq.explain: After CMC the surface is no longer fully wet and the rate falls.

mcq.q: The second falling rate period of drying is controlled by:
options: Movement of moisture from inside to the surface (diffusion/capillary)
mcq.explain: In this period internal moisture movement, not external conditions, limits the rate.

mcq.q: Freeze drying removes water by:
mcq.explain: The frozen product is kept below the triple point so ice turns directly into vapour.

mcq.q: The triple point of water is at:
mcq.explain: Below 4.58 mm Hg ice sublimes directly without melting.

mcq.q: Spray-dried particles are typically:
mcq.explain: Droplets dry from outside in, forming spherical, often hollow, free-flowing particles.

mcq.q: A major hazard of fluidized bed drying of granules wet with organic solvents is:
options: Dust explosion due to static electricity
mcq.explain: Moving fine particles generate static charge; with solvent vapour this can cause explosion, so earthing is needed.

mcq.q: Tumbling blenders such as double cone and V-blender mix powders mainly by:
mcq.explain: Random movement of individual particles over freshly formed surfaces during tumbling is diffusive mixing.

mcq.q: Sigma blade mixer is most suitable for:
mcq.explain: Two sigma blades knead and shear heavy plastic masses.

mcq.q: A propeller mixer mainly produces:
mcq.explain: Propellers move liquid parallel to the shaft (up and down), suitable for low-viscosity liquids.

mcq.q: Vortex formation in a liquid mixing tank is prevented by:
options: Fitting baffles or mounting the impeller off-centre
mcq.explain: Baffles and off-centre/angled mounting convert swirling (tangential) flow into useful axial/radial flow.

mcq.q: The equation that relates filtration rate to the porosity (ε) and specific surface of the cake is:
mcq.explain: Kozeny-Carman: rate ∝ ε³ / [(1-ε)² S²], showing the strong effect of porosity and particle size.

mcq.q: According to Poiseuille's equation, flow rate through a capillary is proportional to:
mcq.explain: dV/dt = πr⁴ΔP / 8ηL; doubling pore radius increases flow 16 times.

mcq.q: Which of the following is a filter aid?
mcq.explain: Kieselguhr is inert and porous and forms a permeable cake.

mcq.q: The pore size of a membrane filter used for sterile filtration is:
mcq.explain: 0.22 µm (or 0.2 µm) membranes retain bacteria; 0.45 µm is used for clarification.

mcq.q: In a plate and frame filter press, the cake collects in the:
mcq.explain: Frames are hollow spaces between plates where solids build up as cake.

mcq.q: In thorough washing in a plate and frame press, the washing plate is marked with:
mcq.explain: Plain plate = one button, frame = two buttons, washing plate = three buttons.

mcq.q: A rotary drum filter is a:
mcq.explain: The drum rotates continuously through filtration, washing, drying and discharge zones under vacuum.

mcq.q: A non-perforated basket centrifuge separates solids by:
mcq.explain: Its solid wall makes solids settle; clear liquid is removed by a skimming tube.

mcq.q: Relative centrifugal force (RCF) in terms of radius r (cm) and speed N (rpm) is:
mcq.explain: RCF = ω²r/g = 1.118 × 10⁻⁵ r N²; it increases with the square of speed.

mcq.q: Corrosion resistance of stainless steel is mainly due to:
mcq.explain: Chromium (at least about 11-12%) forms a thin, self-healing passive oxide layer.

mcq.q: SS 316 differs from SS 304 mainly by the presence of:
mcq.explain: About 2-3% molybdenum improves resistance to chlorides and pitting, so SS 316 is preferred for product-contact parts.

mcq.q: In cathodic protection by the sacrificial anode method, the anode commonly used is:
mcq.explain: A more active metal (Zn, Mg) corrodes in place of the protected steel.

mcq.q: Galvanic corrosion takes place when:
options: A single pure metal is kept in dry air
Two dissimilar metals are in contact in an electrolyte
mcq.explain: The more active metal becomes the anode and corrodes.

mcq.q: Pitting corrosion of stainless steel is mainly promoted by:
mcq.explain: Chlorides break down the passive film at local points, forming deep pits.

mcq.q: Borosilicate glass equipment is attacked by:
mcq.explain: Glass resists most acids but is dissolved by hydrofluoric acid (and hot strong alkalis).

mcq.q: Which of the following is a non-ferrous metal?
mcq.explain: Non-ferrous metals do not contain iron as the main constituent, e.g. aluminium, copper, lead.
